docs.text: Second pdf content

docs.title: Evolution Toward Industry 4.0
docs.text: Before jumping into tech, the PPT usually explains evolution.

docs.title: 1️⃣ Industry 1.0
docs.text:
• Steam power

  • Mechanization

  • Textile mills

docs.title: 2️⃣ Industry 2.0
docs.text:
• Electricity

  • Mass production

  • Assembly lines (think Henry Ford and Ford assembly line)

docs.title: 3️⃣ Industry 3.0
docs.text:
• Electronics

  • PLC

  • Basic automation

  • Computers

docs.title: 4️⃣ Industry 4.0
docs.text:
• Smart factories

  • Data-driven decisions

  • Connected machines

  • Cyber-Physical Systems

Big shift: From automation → to intelligence + connectivity

docs.title: 🧠 SECTION 2 – Cyber Physical Systems (CPS)
docs.text: This is the backbone of Industry 4.0.

docs.title: What is CPS?
docs.text:
A system where:

Physical system + Sensors + Software + Network are tightly integrated.

Example: Smart CNC machine:

  • Sensors measure vibration

  • Data sent to cloud

  • AI predicts tool wear

  • Automatically adjusts cutting speed

That loop is CPS.

docs.title: 1️⃣ Physical Layer
docs.text: Machines, robots, sensors.

docs.title: 2️⃣ Cyber Layer
docs.text: Software, computation, control algorithms.

docs.title: 3️⃣ Communication Layer
docs.text:
IoT, internet, data transfer.

In smart enterprise: Everything is connected continuously.

docs.title: IoT (Internet of Things)
docs.text:
Connecting physical objects to internet.

Examples:

  • Smart fridge

  • Smart thermostat

  • Fitness band

docs.title: IIoT (Industrial IoT)
docs.text:
IoT used in industrial environment.

Example:

  • Temperature sensors in boiler

  • Vibration sensors in motor

  • Real-time production monitoring

Difference: IIoT requires:

  • Higher reliability

  • Security

  • Real-time response

docs.title: IIoT Architecture
docs.text:
Typically includes:

  1. Sensors

  2. Edge devices

  3. Gateway

  4. Cloud platform

  5. Analytics engine

  6. Dashboard

Edge computing means: Processing data near source to reduce latency.

docs.title: ☁ SECTION 4 – Cloud Computing
docs.text:
Cloud allows:

  • Storage

  • Large computation

  • Remote monitoring

  • Global access

Three models:

docs.title: 1️⃣ IaaS
docs.text: Infrastructure as a Service

docs.title: 2️⃣ PaaS
docs.text: Platform as a Service

docs.title: 3️⃣ SaaS
docs.text:
Software as a Service

Example: Using cloud to analyze machine data from multiple factories.

docs.title: 📊 SECTION 5 – Big Data in Smart Enterprises
docs.text:
Industry 4.0 generates massive data.

Types:

  • Structured (tables)

  • Unstructured (images, videos)

  • Streaming data (real-time sensors)

Big Data characterized by:

5 V’s:

  • Volume

  • Velocity

  • Variety

  • Veracity

  • Value

Goal: Convert raw data → actionable insights.

docs.title: 🤖 SECTION 6 – Artificial Intelligence & Machine Learning
docs.text:
AI enables:

  • Predictive maintenance

  • Demand forecasting

  • Quality inspection (vision systems)

  • Production optimization

ML models learn from historical failure data.

Example: Predict motor failure before it happens.

That reduces downtime and cost.

docs.title: 🧬 SECTION 7 – Digital Twin
docs.text: This is one of the most important Industry 4.0 concepts.

docs.title: What is Digital Twin?
docs.text:
A virtual replica of physical system.

Example: Digital twin of turbine:

  • Simulates stress

  • Predicts wear

  • Tests new operating conditions

Before changing real system, you simulate on digital twin.

docs.title: Why Important?
docs.text:
• Reduces risk

  • Faster design iteration

  • Predictive analysis

  • Remote diagnostics

It connects to what we studied in Part-1: Reliability + life cycle cost.

docs.title: 🧵 SECTION 8 – Digital Thread
docs.text:
Digital thread connects:

Design → Manufacturing → Operation → Maintenance → Disposal

All data flows continuously.

So: If field failure happens, design team immediately sees data.

Closed loop engineering.

docs.title: 🏭 SECTION 9 – Smart Factory Characteristics
docs.text:
A smart factory is:

  • Self-optimizing

  • Self-aware

  • Self-configuring

  • Highly flexible

Features:

  • Autonomous robots

  • Real-time monitoring

  • Horizontal integration

  • Vertical integration

docs.title: Horizontal Integration
docs.text: Across supply chain: Supplier ↔ Manufacturer ↔ Distributor

docs.title: Vertical Integration
docs.text: Across company hierarchy: Shop floor ↔ Management ↔ ERP ↔ Strategy

docs.title: 📦 SECTION 10 – Smart Supply Chain
docs.text:
Industry 4.0 enables:

  • Real-time inventory tracking

  • Demand forecasting

  • Just-in-time manufacturing

  • RFID tracking

Example: Amazon warehouses use automation + AI heavily.

docs.title: 💼 SECTION 11 – Smart Enterprise
docs.text:
Smart enterprise is not just smart factory.

It integrates:

  • Manufacturing

  • Finance

  • Marketing

  • Logistics

  • Customer data

Everything connected digitally.

Decisions based on real-time analytics.

docs.title: 💰 SECTION 12 – Business Models in Industry 4.0
docs.text:
Shift from:

Product selling → Service-based model

Example: Instead of selling engine, company sells “Power by the hour”.

Predictive maintenance enabled by sensors.

Revenue becomes: Subscription-based.

docs.title: ⚠ SECTION 13 – Challenges in Industry 4.0
docs.text:
Very important for exams.

  1. Cybersecurity risk

  2. High initial investment

  3. Skill gap

  4. Integration with legacy systems

  5. Data privacy

  6. Standardization issues

Smart enterprise requires: Organizational change + technical change.

docs.title: 🌍 SECTION 14 – Sustainability & Industry 4.0
docs.text:
Smart systems help:

  • Reduce waste

  • Energy optimization

  • Carbon footprint tracking

  • Circular economy

Sensors monitor energy usage. AI optimizes consumption.

docs.title: 🔐 SECTION 15 – Cybersecurity
docs.text:
Critical in IIoT.

Threats:

  • Data theft

  • System hacking

  • Industrial espionage

Requires:

  • Encryption

  • Authentication

  • Secure protocols

  • Firewalls

docs.title: 🎯 Big Picture Summary of Part-2
docs.text:
Industry 4.0 is integration of:

Physical systems

  • Digital systems

  • Data analytics

  • AI

  • Cloud

  • Connectivity

To create:

Smart factories → Smart enterprises → Smart economy

docs.text:
• Is a Structural Design Pattern
  • Also known as wrapper pattern
  • An adapter allows incompatible interfaces to work together
  • It converts one interface into another that the client expects
Role Meaning Client Existing code that expects some interface Target The interface the client expects Adaptee Existing / new / legacy class with incompatible interface Adapter The translator between Target and Adaptee >Adapter adapts the adaptee to the target interface
  • Client knows only Target
  • Adapter implements Target
  • Adapter internally calls Adaptee
  • Client thinks it's talking to Target
  • In reality, its talking to the Adapter
  • Adapter delegates to Adaptee

docs.title: Object Adapter
docs.text:
• Adapter has an instance of Adaptee
  • Adapter delegates to the adaptee instance
interface Target {
    void request();
}

class Adaptee {
    public void specificRequest() {
        System.out.println("Specific Request");
    }
}

class ObjectAdapter implements Target {
    private Adaptee adaptee;

    public ObjectAdapter(Adaptee adaptee) {
        this.adaptee = adaptee;
    }

    @Override
    public void request() {
        adaptee.specificRequest();
    }
}

class Client {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Adaptee adaptee = new Adaptee();
        Target target = new ObjectAdapter(adaptee);

        target.request();
    }
}

docs.title: Class Adapter
docs.text:
• Adapter is-a Adaptee
  • Adapter pretends to be Target
class ClassAdapter extends Adapter implements Target {
    @Override
    public void request() {
        specificRequest();
    }
}

class Client {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Target target = new ClassAdapter();

        target.request();
    }
}

docs.title: Universal Adapter
docs.text:
• One adapter
  • Multiple adaptees
  • Chosen at runtime
  • Since object adapter uses composition, it can take as many adaptees as needed

docs.title: Design Patterns
docs.text:
• Creational
  • Structural
  • Behavioral

docs.title: Creational
docs.text:
• Decouple object creation from object usage
  • Control, hide or optimize object creation
Pattern What it does Singleton Only one instance Factory Method Subclass decides object Abstract Factory Create families of objects Builder Step-by-step object creation Prototype Clone existing object # Structural - How should classes and objects be composed - Deal with relationships between classes and objects Pattern What it does Adapter Convert interface Facade Simplify interface Decorator Add behavior dynamically Composite Tree structures Proxy Control access Bridge Separate abstraction & implementation Flyweight Share objects # Behavioral - How do objects communicate and behave - Defines communication patterns between objects Pattern What it does Observer Notify dependents Strategy Switch algorithms Command Encapsulate requests State Change behavior by state Template Method Skeleton of algorithm Iterator Traverse collections Mediator Central communication Chain of Responsibility Pass request along chain Visitor Separate operations Memento Save & restore state Aspect Creational Structural Behavioral Focus Object creation Object structure Object interaction Answers How to create? How to connect? How to communicate? Scope Mostly classes Classes & objects Mostly objects Goal Reduce coupling in creation Simplify structure Simplify behavior Example Factory Adapter Observer

docs.title: Facade
docs.text:
• Is a Structural Design Pattern
  • Facade provides a simple, unified interface to a complex subsystem
  • It hides the complexity and gives you a single easy entry point
  • Create one class that:
    • Knows the subsystem
    • Coordinates the calls
    • Exposes a simple API

docs.title: When to use
docs.text:
• Subsystem is complex
  • Client code is messy
  • For loose coupling
  • To expose a clean API
Engine engine = new Engine();
engine.start();

FuelInjector injector = new FuelInjector();
injector.inject();

AirFlowController air = new AirFlowController();
air.control();

CarStarter starter = new CarStarter();
starter.start();

class CarFacade {
    private Engine engine = new Engine();
    private FuelInjector injector = new FuelInjector();
    private AirFlowController airFlow = new AirFlowController();

    void startCar() {
        engine.start();
        injector.inject();
        airFlow.control();
        System.out.println("Car started");
    }
}

public class Client {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        CarFacade car = new CarFacade();
        car.startCar();
    }
}

docs.title: Observer
docs.text:
• Is a behavioral pattern
  • Observer defines a one to many dependency so that when one object changes state, all its dependents are notified automatically
  • One object publishes changes, many objects react

docs.title: Solves
docs.text:
• Tight coupling
  • Need to explicitly know who all to notify
  • Adding / Removing listeners difficulty
Role Responsibility Subject Maintains list of observers ConcreteSubject Holds state Observer Interface for notification ConcreteObserver Reacts to changes 
interface Observer {
    void update(int temperature);
}

interface Subject {
    void registerObserver(Observer o);
    void removeObserver(Observer o);
    void notifyObservers();
}

class WeatherStation implements Subject {
    private List<Observer> observers = new ArrayList<>();
    private int temperature;

    public void setTemperature(int temp) {
        this.temperature = temp;
        notifyObservers();
    }

    @Override
    public void registerObserver(Observer o) {
        this.observers.add(o);
    }

    @Override
    public void removeObserver(Observer o) {
        this.observers.remove(o);
    }

    @Override
    public void notifyObservers() {
        for (Observer o : observers) {
            o.update(temperature);
        }
    }
}

class PhoneDisplay implements Observer {
    @Override
    public void update(int temperature) {
        System.out.println("updated temp in phone display");
    }
}

class TVDisplay implements Observer {
    @Override
    public void update(int temperature) {
        System.out.println("updated temp in TV display");
    }
}

class Client {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        WeatherStation station = new WeatherStation();
        Observer phone = new PhoneDisplay();
        Observer tv = new TVDisplay();

        station.registerObserver(phone);
        station.registerObserver(tv);

        station.setTemperature(10);
        station.setTemperature(20);
    }
}
  • There will be two interfaces corresponding to
    • Observer
    • Subject
  • And two or more implementations for the same

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
• Subject keep track of the observers
  • When generates the events
    • It loops through the observers
    • notify each of the observers
  • We can keep a get and set state methods in the concrete implementation of subject if the observers need to get some data from the subject on notification

docs.title: 🔹 What is a Business Case?
docs.text:
A business case is:

A formal justification for starting a project.

It answers one main question:

“Why should we do this project?”

Before investing money, time, and people, management wants proof that:

  • The project is worth it

  • The benefits justify the cost

  • The risks are acceptable

That justification document is the business case.

docs.title: 🔹 Simple Real-Life Analogy
docs.text:
Suppose a company wants to build a new food delivery app.

Before development, management asks:

  • How much will it cost?

  • How many users will use it?

  • What is the expected profit?

  • Who are competitors?

  • What are the risks?

The document answering these is the business case.

docs.title: 🔹 What Does a Business Case Contain?
docs.text: Now let’s go section by section.

docs.title: 1. Project Background
docs.text:
• What problem are we solving?

  • Why does it matter?

Example: Customers face delays in ordering medicines online.

docs.title: 2. Business Opportunity
docs.text:
• What are we trying to achieve?
  • What difference will it make?
  • What if we don't do it?

Examples:

  • Increase revenue by 20%

  • Reduce manual processing cost

  • Improve customer satisfaction

docs.title: 3. Cost Estimation
docs.text:
Includes:

  • Development cost

  • Infrastructure cost

  • Maintenance cost

  • Training cost

  • Operational cost

Often includes:

  • ROI (Return on Investment)

  • Payback period

docs.title: 4. Benefits (Very Important)
docs.text: Two types:

docs.title: 🔹 Tangible Benefits (measurable)
docs.text:
• Increased revenue

  • Reduced cost

  • Time savings

docs.title: 🔹 Intangible Benefits (non-measurable)
docs.text:
• Brand value

  • Customer trust

  • Market reputation

docs.title: 5. Risk Analysis
docs.text:
• Technical risks

  • Financial risks

  • Market risks

  • Operational risks

Example:

  • Technology may fail

  • Market demand may be low

  • Competitor may dominate

docs.title: 🔹 Structure Summary
docs.text:
A typical business case includes:

  1. Project Background

  2. Business Opportunity

  3. Costs

  4. Benefits

  5. Risks

docs.title: 🔥 Important Clarification
docs.text:
Business Case ≠ Project Plan

Business Case: Should we do it?

Project Plan: How will we do it?

docs.title: 🔹 Why Business Case Is Critical
docs.text:
Because software projects fail mainly due to:

  • Wrong market assumptions

  • Overestimated benefits

  • Underestimated cost

  • Ignored risks

A strong business case prevents that.

docs.title: 🔹 Example (Mini Case)
docs.text:
Suppose a bank wants to automate loan approval.

Business Case may show:

Cost: $2 million Annual savings: $1 million Payback period: 2 years Risk: Medium Feasibility: High

Management approves.

Without business case → blind investment.

docs.title: 🔹 Clean Exam Definition
docs.text: A business case is a formal document that provides justification for undertaking a project by evaluating its benefits, costs, risks, and feasibility.

docs.title: 1. What is Computer Systems Engineering?
docs.text:
While Software Engineering focuses only on the programs (code), Computer Systems Engineering is a broader field that includes both the software and the physical hardware it runs on.

  • Encompasses Software Engineering: You can think of Software Engineering as one of the major parts inside the "umbrella" of Computer Systems Engineering.
  • The Goal: To build products that need a custom physical body (hardware) and a brain to control it (software).

docs.title: 2. The "Big Decision": Hardware-Software Partitioning
docs.text:
The most important step in this field is called Partitioning. This is when engineers sit down and decide:

  1. What should the hardware do? (e.g., physical sensors, buttons, power supply).
  2. What should the software do? (e.g., calculating data, showing a menu on a screen).

docs.title: Example: A Coffee Vending Machine
docs.text:
• Hardware Tasks: The physical boiler to heat water, the tubes to pour the coffee, and the coin slot to detect money.
  • Software Tasks: Counting how much money was inserted, checking if the water is hot enough yet, and telling the hardware exactly when to stop pouring the milk.

docs.title: 3. How the Development Process Works
docs.text: In general software engineering, you usually have the computer (hardware) ready. In Computer Systems Engineering, you are building both at the same time.

docs.title: The Step-by-Step Workflow:
docs.text:
1. Feasibility Study: Can we actually build this? Is it worth the money?.
  2. Requirements Analysis: What exactly does the customer want the system to do?.
  3. Hardware-Software Partitioning: Deciding which tasks are for hardware and which are for software.
  4. Parallel Development: This is the clever part. Both teams start working at the same time:
    • The Hardware Team builds the physical circuit boards and parts.
    • The Software Team writes the code. Since the hardware isn't finished yet, they often use a Hardware Simulator (a computer program that acts like the real machine) to test their code.
  5. Integration: The finished software is loaded onto the finished hardware.
  6. System Testing: The final check to see if the hardware and software work perfectly together as one single system.

docs.title: 4. Real-World Examples
docs.text:
Many modern products are results of Computer Systems Engineering:

  • Robotic Toys: The plastic body and motors (hardware) controlled by a program that tells the toy how to walk (software).
  • Health Bands (Smart Watches): The heart-rate sensors and battery (hardware) working with an app that tracks your steps and sleep (software).
  • Microwave Ovens: The physical magnetron that heats food (hardware) and the digital timer and touch-pad menu (software).

docs.title: 5. Summary Table
docs.text:
Feature Software Engineering (SE) Computer Systems Engineering (CSE) Focus Just the program/code. Both hardware and software. Main Task Designing logic and data. Partitioning tasks between HW and SW. Testing Done on existing computers. Done using HW Simulators first, then real HW. Result An app or program. A physical device (like a robot or machine).

Note: In the provided sources, "Computer Systems Engineering" is described as the overarching discipline that includes Software Engineering as a sub-component when building hardware-specific products.

docs.title: 🔹 First: Where Are We in the Life Cycle?
docs.text:
In models like the Waterfall model, after:

  1. Feasibility

  2. Requirements Analysis (SRS)

comes:

3️⃣ Design Phase

Design answers:

“How will we build the system?”

Not what (that was requirements), but how.

docs.title: 💡 What is Structured Analysis?
docs.text:
Structured analysis is:

A systematic way of analyzing requirements by modeling the system logically before designing it physically.

It focuses on:

  • What the system should do

  • How data flows

  • What processing happens

It is still logical — not technical implementation yet.

docs.title: 🧠 Key Idea
docs.text:
We convert requirements into models.

These models represent:

  • Data flow

  • Processes

  • Data stores

  • External entities

docs.title: 1️⃣ Data Flow Diagrams (DFDs)
docs.text:
Shows:

  • How data moves

  • What processes transform data

Example:

Customer → Place Order → Order Database

docs.title: 2️⃣ Entity-Relationship (ER) Diagrams
docs.text:
Shows:

  • Data entities

  • Relationships

  • Attributes

Example:

Customer — places — Order

docs.title: 3️⃣ Data Dictionary
docs.text:
Defines:

  • Meaning of each data item

  • Format

  • Structure

docs.title: 🎯 Purpose of Structured Analysis
docs.text:
• Understand system logically

  • Remove ambiguity

  • Break complex system into smaller processes

  • Prepare foundation for design

docs.title: 🔥 Important
docs.text:
Structured analysis answers:

What functions exist? What data exists? How does data move?

It does NOT answer:

  • Which programming language?

  • Which database?

  • Which server?

docs.title: 🔹 2️⃣ Structured Design
docs.text: Now we move from logical understanding to physical structure.

docs.title: 💡 What is Structured Design?
docs.text:
Structured design is:

Transforming the logical models into a structured solution architecture.

This is where we decide:

  • Modules

  • Interfaces

  • Control flow

  • Data structures

docs.title: 🧠 Core Idea
docs.text:
We apply:

  • Decomposition

  • Abstraction

  • Modularity

We break the system into modules.

docs.title: 1️⃣ Top-Down Design
docs.text:
Start with:

Main System

Break into:

Subsystems → Modules → Submodules

Like:

Online Shopping System → Order Module → Payment Module → Inventory Module

docs.title: 2️⃣ Structure Charts
docs.text:
Shows:

  • Module hierarchy

  • Calling relationships

  • Data flow between modules

docs.title: 3️⃣ Cohesion & Coupling Principles
docs.text:
Good design ensures:

  • High cohesion (module does one thing well)

  • Low coupling (modules are independent)

docs.title: 🎯 Purpose of Structured Design
docs.text:
• Convert analysis models into implementable design

  • Define architecture

  • Prepare blueprint for coding

docs.title: 🔥 Important Difference
docs.text: Structured Analysis Structured Design Logical view Physical/architectural view What system does How system is built DFDs, ER diagrams Structure charts, module design

docs.title: 🔹 3️⃣ Design Review
docs.text: Now comes quality control.

docs.title: 💡 What is Design Review?
docs.text:
Design review is:

A formal evaluation of the design to detect errors before coding begins.

This is very important.

Because:

Fixing errors in design is MUCH cheaper than fixing in coding.

docs.title: 🧠 Why Review is Needed
docs.text:
If design has flaw:

  • Code will have flaw

  • Testing will find it late

  • Cost increases exponentially

Remember:

Modern SE emphasizes: 👉 Error prevention over error correction.

docs.title: 🔍 What Happens in Design Review?
docs.text:
Team checks:

  • Is design consistent with requirements?

  • Are modules properly defined?

  • Are interfaces clear?

  • Any missing functionality?

  • Any unnecessary complexity?

docs.title: 🧑‍🤝‍🧑 Who Participates?
docs.text:
• Designers

  • Senior engineers

  • Project manager

  • Sometimes client

docs.title: 📋 Types of Review
docs.text:
• Informal review

  • Walkthrough

  • Formal technical review (FTR)

docs.title: 🎯 Goal of Design Review
docs.text:
• Detect logical errors

  • Detect architectural weaknesses

  • Improve quality

  • Reduce future maintenance cost

docs.title: 🔥 Big Picture Flow
docs.text:
During Design Phase:

Step 1 → Structured Analysis Understand the system logically.

Step 2 → Structured Design Convert logic into architecture.

Step 3 → Design Review Verify and validate design before coding.

docs.title: 🔥 Why This Matters in Exams
docs.text:
Many students confuse:

Analysis vs Design

Golden Rule:

  • Analysis = Problem understanding

  • Design = Solution planning

docs.title: 🧠 Real-Life Analogy
docs.text:
Imagine building a hospital.

Structured Analysis:

  • How many patients?

  • What departments needed?

  • What services offered?

Structured Design:

  • How many floors?

  • Where is ICU?

  • Electrical layout?

  • Plumbing layout?

Design Review:

  • Engineers check blueprint.

  • Ensure structure is safe.

  • Ensure no design mistakes.

Only after this → Construction begins.

docs.title: 🎯 Final Clean Summary
docs.text:
Structured Analysis: Logical modeling of system functions and data.

Structured Design: Architectural breakdown into modules and implementation plan.

Design Review: Formal checking of design for correctness and quality.

docs.title: Evolution of Other SE Techniques
docs.text: Beyond just the ways we design code (like Object-Oriented or Data Flow design), several other essential techniques have evolved to help engineers build high-quality software. These techniques help manage the team, ensure the software works, and keep the project on track.

docs.title: 1. Life Cycle Models (SDLC)
docs.text:
A Software Life Cycle Model is a descriptive "map" or recipe for the development process. It tells the team exactly what activities to do and in what order.

  • Why use it? It prevents chaos in team environments by ensuring everyone knows "when to do what".
  • Examples:
    • Waterfall Model: Doing one stage at a time (Plan -> Design -> Code -> Test).
    • Agile Models: Working in small, quick "sprints" to deliver pieces of software every few weeks.
  • Simple Example: Think of it like building a house. You follow a specific life cycle: first you clear the land, then lay the foundation, then build walls, and finally paint. You wouldn't paint before the walls are up!

docs.title: 2. Specification Techniques
docs.text:
These techniques focus on gathering and writing down exactly what the customer needs before any coding begins.

  • The Goal: To create a Software Requirements Specification (SRS) document that acts as a contract between the developer and the user.
  • Simple Example: If a client says, "I want a fast app," the specification technique helps define that as "The app must load the home screen in under 2 seconds".

docs.title: 3. Project Management Techniques
docs.text:
Building software isn't just about writing code; it's about managing people, time, and money.

  • Key Tasks: Estimation (how much will it cost?), Scheduling (how long will it take?), and Monitoring (are we on track?).
  • Simple Example: A project manager uses these techniques to realize that a project is 2 weeks behind schedule and decides to move two extra developers to help finish the "login" feature on time.

docs.title: 4. Testing & Debugging Techniques
docs.text:
These are systematic ways to find and fix mistakes (bugs).

  • Testing: Checking if the software does what it is supposed to do. This includes Unit Testing (testing small parts) and System Testing (testing the whole thing).
  • Debugging: The "detective work" of finding out why a specific error happened and fixing the root cause.
  • Simple Example: A Unit Test checks if the "Submit" button works. If it doesn't, Debugging is used to find out that a single line of code was missing a semicolon.

docs.title: 5. Quality Assurance (QA) Techniques
docs.text:
QA techniques are used to ensure the final product is reliable and meets high standards.

  • Key Principle: Phase Containment of Errors. This means catching a mistake in the same stage where it was made. Catching a design mistake during the "Design Phase" is 10x cheaper than catching it after the software is finished.
  • Simple Example: Having a "Code Review" where a second programmer looks at your work to find mistakes before the code is ever even tested.

docs.title: 6. Software Metrics
docs.text:
Metrics are "rulers" used to measure the software and the process.

  • The Goal: To use numbers to see if the project is getting better or worse.
  • Examples:
    • Counting the number of bugs found per 1,000 lines of code.
    • Measuring how much money (cost) is spent on each feature.
  • Simple Example: Like a fitness tracker for a project. If the "bug count" goes up every week, the team knows they need to slow down and focus on quality.

docs.title: 7. CASE Tools (Computer-Aided Software Engineering)
docs.text:
CASE tools are specialized software programs that help engineers perform their jobs more efficiently.

  • How they help: They can automatically draw diagrams, generate code, or track bugs.
  • Simple Example: Instead of drawing a database plan on a piece of paper, an engineer uses a CASE tool to draw it on a computer. The tool can then automatically create the actual database code from that drawing.

docs.title: 8. Modern Design Extensions
docs.text:
In recent years, design techniques have evolved further from standard Object-Oriented design into more specialized styles:

  • Component-Based Development: Building software by plugging together pre-made "parts" (components), like building with Lego bricks.
  • Service-Oriented Architecture (SOA): Designing software as a collection of "services" that talk to each other over a network.
  • Aspect-Oriented Programming: Focusing on "cross-cutting" concerns, like security, that affect every part of the program.
Component-Based SOA Usually within same application Distributed over network Often same runtime Can be different platforms Tight integration Loose coupling Local communication Network communication Approach Focus OOP Objects and their responsibilities Component-Based Reusable building blocks SOA Distributed services AOP Cross-cutting concerns

docs.title: Evolution of SE Techniques
docs.text: Software development has changed significantly over the decades. It moved from being an individual "art" to a disciplined "engineering" profession. This evolution was driven by the need to handle the exponential growth in complexity as programs became larger.

docs.title: 1. Early Computer Programming (1950s)
docs.text:
In the beginning, programming was more of an art or a craft than a science.

  • Style: Programs were written in Assembly language.
  • Size: Very small, usually only a few hundred lines of code.
  • Method: This was the era of Exploratory Programming (also called the build-and-fix style).
  • Problem: Every programmer had their own personal style based on intuition. There were no set rules, making it almost impossible for one person to understand code written by someone else.

docs.title: 2. High-Level Language Programming (Early 1960s)
docs.text:
The introduction of languages like FORTRAN, ALGOL, and COBOL made writing code much easier and faster.

  • Progress: Program sizes grew to a few thousand lines.
  • Remaining Issue: Even though the languages were better, the development style was still "exploratory" and lacked a systematic approach.

docs.title: 3. Control Flow-Based Design (Late 1960s)
docs.text:
As programs got bigger, they became "spaghetti code"—messy and hard to follow. To fix this, experts focused on the Control Structure (the sequence in which instructions are executed).

  • The Problem: Excessive use of GO TO statements (or JUMP instructions) made programs impossible to debug or understand.
  • The Solution: In 1969, Dijkstra published "Goto Statement Considered Harmful," leading to the birth of Structured Programming.
  • The Three Pillars: It was proved that any logic could be written using only three structures:
    1. Sequence: Statements happen one after another.
    2. Selection: Making decisions (if-then-else).
    3. Iteration: Repeating actions (loops like while/do-while).

docs.title: 4. Data Structure-Oriented Design (Early 1970s)
docs.text:
Engineers realized that for very large programs, the data was more important than the instructions.

  • Main Idea: The structure of the code should mirror the structure of the data it processes.
  • Example: Jackson's Structured Programming (JSP) methodology. Here, you first design the data structures and then use that design to derive the program's code structure.

docs.title: 5. Data Flow-Oriented Design (Late 1970s)
docs.text:
This technique treats a system like a processing factory.

  • Main Idea: Focus on how data "flows" through the system from input to output.
  • The Process:
    1. Identify the input data.
    2. Identify the "processing stations" (functions) that change the data.
    3. Identify the final output.
  • Example: A Car Assembly Unit. You track the "Chassis" as it flows through stations like "Fit Engine" and "Fit Wheels" to become a "Finished Car".

docs.title: 6. Object-Oriented Design (1980s)
docs.text:
This is the most popular modern approach. It organizes software around real-world objects rather than functions.

  • Main Idea: Instead of thinking about "how to calculate payroll," you think about "The Employee," "The Manager," and "The Department".
  • Key Features:
    • Data Hiding: Objects keep their data private and safe.
    • Relationships: Objects interact through inheritance, composition, and references.
  • Benefits: It makes code simpler to reuse, easier to maintain, and more robust.

docs.title: 7. Summary of the Evolution
docs.text:
The journey of design techniques can be mapped as follows: Ad hoc (Build-and-fix) → Control flow-based → Data structure-based → Data flow-based → Object-Oriented.

From the 1980s onwards, OOD further evolved into specialized areas like Component-based development and Service-oriented architectures.

docs.title: Key Shift: Exploratory vs. Modern SE
docs.text: Feature Exploratory Style (Old) Modern SE Practices (New) Focus Coding is the main activity. Coding is just a small part of the effort. Errors Detected only during testing. Prevention and detection in every phase. Planning Very little/informal. Rigorous planning, estimation, and monitoring. Documentation Sparse and poor quality. Consistent, high-quality documentation.

docs.title: Exploratory vs Modern Software Development
docs.text: The transition from early programming to modern software engineering reflects a shift from an individual "art" or "craft" to a disciplined engineering approach. This move was necessary to handle the increasing complexity of software that humans can no longer manage using unorganized methods.

docs.title: 1. The Exploratory Style (Build-and-Fix)
docs.text:
Used primarily by early programmers and beginners, the exploratory style is often called the "build-and-fix" approach.

  • How it Works: A programmer quickly develops a "dirty" program without much planning. Once the code is running, the programmer tests it and fixes bugs only as they are noticed.
  • Best For: This style can only be used successfully for very small (toy) programs that one person can easily keep in their head.
  • The Problem (Exponential Effort): As the program gets larger, the effort, time, and cost required to finish it grow exponentially. Eventually, the problem becomes so complex that it exceeds the human brain's "grasping power," causing the approach to break down completely.
  • Team Impact: It is very difficult to use this style in a team because there is no common understanding of "when to do what," leading to chaos and project failure.

Example: A student writing a 50-line script to calculate their GPA. They start coding immediately, run it, see an error, change a line, and repeat until it works. No documents or blueprints are ever made.

docs.title: 2. Modern Software Development Practice
docs.text:
Modern practices use Software Engineering (SE) principles to ensure that software is built in a systematic, disciplined, and measurable way.

  • How it Works: Software is developed through several well-defined stages, such as Requirements Analysis, Design, Coding, and Testing. This is known as a Software Life Cycle Model (like the Waterfall or Agile models).
  • Focus on Prevention: While exploratory style focuses on correcting errors after they happen, modern practices focus on error prevention.
  • Phase Containment of Errors: Modern developers try to detect errors in the same phase they were introduced. For example, finding a mistake in the "Design" phase is much cheaper than finding it during final "Testing".
  • Role of Coding: In the exploratory style, coding is the development. In modern SE, coding is only a small part of the total effort; more time is spent on planning, specifying requirements, and designing the architecture.

Example: A team building a mobile banking app. They first spend weeks talking to users (Requirements), then create blueprints of the database and screens (Design), and only then start writing code. They use CASE tools to help plan and monitor their progress.

docs.title: 3. Key Differences at a Glance
docs.text: Feature Exploratory Style (Build-and-Fix) Modern Software Engineering Effort Curve Exponential: Costs explode as the program grows. Linear: Effort stays manageable even for large systems. Error Handling Detects errors only during testing. Phase Containment: Detects errors as soon as they are made. Documentation Very little or sparse documentation. Produces consistent, standard documents (like an SRS). Main Activity Coding is the primary task. Coding is just one small stage of many. Visibility Low: Only the programmer knows the status. High: Managers can track progress through milestones. Teamwork Leads to chaos in team environments. Life cycle models provide a precise understanding for the team.

docs.title: 4. Human Cognition: Why Modern SE Wins
docs.text:
Modern SE techniques are specifically designed to overcome human cognitive limitations. Research shows that human short-term memory can only hold about 7 items at once.

  • Exploratory style fails because as a program grows, there are too many variables and logic paths for a human to track at once.
  • Modern SE uses Abstraction (ignoring unnecessary details) and Decomposition (breaking a big problem into small chapters) to keep the project within the brain's "grasping power".

docs.title: Feasibility Study
docs.text: The Feasibility Study is the very first step in the software development process. Before a company spends millions of dollars and months of time, they need to make sure the project is actually a good idea.

docs.title: 1. What is a Feasibility Study?
docs.text:
The main goal of this study is to determine if a project is technically possible and financially worthwhile.

Essentially, you are trying to answer three big questions:

  1. Can we build it? (Technical)
  2. Should we build it? (Economic)
  3. Can we finish it in time? (Schedule)

The result of this stage is a Feasibility Report, which helps managers make a "Go/No-Go" decision.

docs.title: 2. The Three Dimensions of Feasibility
docs.text: According to the sources, we look at feasibility through three lenses:

docs.title: I. Technical Feasibility
docs.text:
We check if we have the "brainpower" and the "tools" to do the job.

  • Questions: Do we have the right programming skills? Is the technology (like a specific database or hardware) available?
  • Example: If a client wants an AI that can predict the future with 100% accuracy, the study would find this technically infeasible because that technology doesn't exist yet.

docs.title: II. Economic Feasibility (Cost-Benefit Analysis)
docs.text:
This is all about the money. We compare the Costs of making the software against the Benefits it will bring.

  • Costs: Development price, setting up servers, training staff, and daily operations.
  • Benefits: Increased sales, saving time, or reducing errors.
  • The Rule: The benefits must be greater than the costs.

docs.title: III. Schedule Feasibility
docs.text:
We check the clock. Can we finish the project by the customer's deadline?.

  • Example: If a company needs a tax-filing app ready by April, but the study shows it will take 8 months to build, the project is schedule infeasible.

docs.title: 3. Activities During the Study
docs.text:
To complete the study, a manager or analyst performs these steps:

  1. Understand the Problem: Get a rough idea of what the customer wants (what data goes in, what comes out).
  2. Propose Solutions: Think of 2 or 3 different ways to build the system.
  3. Compare Alternatives: Look at the cost and time for each different solution.
  4. Perform Cost-Benefit Analysis: Pick the best solution and prove it will save/make money.

docs.title: 4. Case Study: The Mining Company (CFL)
docs.text:
The sources provide an excellent example involving a mining company called CFL.

  • The Problem: CFL has over 50,000 workers. Mining is dangerous, and casualties are high. The current system for paying benefits (SPF) is too slow, and families are suffering while waiting for money.
  • The Feasibility Study Process:
    1. The manager visits the main office to see what the system needs to do.
    2. The manager visits the actual mine site to see how data is collected.
    3. The manager suggests a few different ways to build a faster software system.
    4. The manager presents the best solution to the officials.
  • The Decision: The officials look at the report and decide "Go" (start the project) or "No-Go" (cancel it).

docs.title: 5. Cost Benefit Analysis
docs.text:
• Identify the costs
    1. Development costs
    2. Setup cost
    3. Operational cost
  • Identify the benefits
    1. Quantifiable
    2. Non Quantifiable
  • Check whether benefit > cost

docs.title: 6. Summary Table
docs.text:
Feature Description When it happens At the very start of the life cycle. Main Document Feasibility Report. Economic Goal Benefits must outweigh the costs. Key Risk If you skip this, you might waste millions on a project that can't be finished.

Note: In the sources, "Economic Feasibility" and "Cost-Benefit Analysis" are often used interchangeably because the financial "worth" is usually the deciding factor for businesses.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: Welcome to the world of Software Engineering (SE)! This note explains what software engineering is, why we need it, and how it helps us build big, complex programs without losing our minds.

docs.title: 1. What is Software Engineering?
docs.text:
In simple terms, Software Engineering is the organized and scientific way of building software.

  • The IEEE Definition: It is a systematic, disciplined, and measurable approach to developing and fixing software.
  • The Building Analogy: Think of it like building a massive skyscraper. You don't just start stacking bricks. You need blueprints, physics, specialized tools, and a plan. Software Engineering is the "blueprint and physics" for apps and programs.

docs.title: 2. The "Software Crisis"
docs.text: For a long time, the world has faced a "Software Crisis" because building good software is surprisingly hard.

docs.title: Common Problems:
docs.text:
• Requirements fail: The software doesn't do what the user actually needs.
  • Expensive: It costs way more than planned.
  • Late: It is rarely finished on time.
  • Messy: It is hard to fix (debug) or change later.

Real-world Stat: According to the Standish Group, only about 28% of software projects are successful. The rest are either cancelled or finish late and over budget.

docs.title: 3. Why Software? (Hardware vs. Software)
docs.text:
If software is so hard to make, why don't we just use hardware?

Feature Hardware Software Flexibility Very hard to change once built. Relatively easy and fast to change. Physicality Heavy, takes up space, uses power. No weight, no space, uses almost no power. Cost Trend Getting cheaper every year. Getting more expensive because of human labor.

docs.title: 4. The Evolution: From Art to Engineering
docs.text:
Programming has changed over time in three steps:

  1. Art: In the beginning, it was like magic. Only a few "artists" knew how to do it based on their own secret experiences.
  2. Craft: It became a skill people learned, but it was still unorganized.
  3. Engineering: Today, we use scientific rules and past experiences in a systematic way to make sure the software is cost-effective and high quality.

docs.title: 5. How Our Brain Works (Human Cognition)
docs.text:
To understand why we need engineering, we have to look at how humans think. Our brain has two types of memory:

  • Long-term Memory: A huge storage for everything we know.
  • Short-term Memory: A tiny "workspace" where we process active thoughts.

docs.title: The "Magical Number 7"
docs.text:
Research shows our short-term memory can only hold about 7 items (plus or minus 2) at once.

  • Example: If I give you 5 variables to track in a program, you’re fine. If I give you 50, your brain "crashes" because it can't hold them all in that tiny workspace.

docs.title: Chunking
docs.text:
We can "cheat" this limit by grouping information into chunks.

  • Example: It’s hard to remember 110010101001 as individual digits. But if you group them into four sets of three (110) (010) (101) (001), it only takes up 4 slots in your memory instead of 12.

docs.title: 6. How Software Engineering Handles Complexity
docs.text: Because our brains are limited, SE uses two main tricks to keep large projects simple:

docs.title: I. Abstraction
docs.text:
Abstraction means focusing only on what is important and ignoring the unnecessary details.

  • Example (The Map): A road map is an "abstraction" of a country. It doesn't show every single tree or house because that would be confusing. It only shows the roads you need for driving.

docs.title: II. Decomposition
docs.text:
Decomposition means breaking one big, scary problem into many small, easy-to-understand parts.

  • Example (The Bundle of Sticks): It is impossible to break a thick bundle of sticks all at once. But if you untie the bundle and break each stick one by one, it is very easy.

docs.title: 🔹 PART 2: Job vs Project vs Exploration
docs.text:
This is about nature of work, not software type.

This classification is based on uncertainty and repeatability.

docs.title: 🟢 1. Job
docs.text:
A job is:

A repetitive, well-defined activity with very little uncertainty.

docs.title: Characteristics:
docs.text:
• Same task repeated

  • Clearly defined steps

  • No creativity required

  • Predictable outcome

docs.title: Examples:
docs.text:
• Data entry

  • Payroll processing

  • Running a backup daily

  • Printing reports

Outcome is almost guaranteed.

Very low uncertainty.

docs.title: 🔵 2. Project
docs.text:
A project is:

A temporary effort to create a unique product, service, or result.

It is between job and exploration.

docs.title: Characteristics:
docs.text:
• Has start and end

  • Defined goal

  • Some uncertainty

  • Some creativity required

  • Combination of routine + new challenges

docs.title: Examples:
docs.text:
• Developing a hospital management system

  • Building a new mobile app

  • Creating a new website

Projects have:

  • Scope

  • Budget

  • Timeline

Software development is considered a project.

docs.title: 🔴 3. Exploration
docs.text:
An exploration is:

A highly uncertain activity where outcome is not guaranteed.

docs.title: Characteristics:
docs.text:
• Research-based

  • Unknown results

  • Experimental

  • No guaranteed success

docs.title: Examples:
docs.text:
• Finding cure for cancer

  • Discovering new AI algorithm

  • Scientific research

  • Space exploration

You don’t know:

  • Whether it will succeed

  • When it will succeed

  • What exact result will come

Very high uncertainty.

docs.title: 🔥 Visual Understanding
docs.text:
Imagine uncertainty on a scale:

Low → Medium → High

Job → Project → Exploration

docs.title: 🔎 Deep Conceptual Difference
docs.text: Factor Job Project Exploration Uncertainty Very Low Medium Very High Repeatability High Low None Creativity Minimal Moderate Very High Outcome Guaranteed Likely Unknown Duration Ongoing Temporary Undefined

docs.title: 🔥 Important Insight
docs.text:
Software Engineering mainly deals with Projects, not jobs and not pure exploration.

Why?

Because:

  • It has defined deliverables

  • It has constraints

  • It requires planning

  • It has uncertainty but manageable

docs.title: 🎯 Real-Life Example
docs.text:
Suppose a company wants to build a new AI-based fraud detection system.

  • Writing same SQL query daily → Job

  • Building the fraud detection system → Project

  • Researching new AI theory for fraud prediction → Exploration

See the difference?

docs.title: Job vs Project vs Exploration:
docs.text:
• Job = Routine, low uncertainty

  • Project = Unique, temporary, moderate uncertainty

  • Exploration = Research, high uncertainty

docs.title: Maintenance
docs.text: Development effort : Maintenance Effort = 40 : 60

docs.title: - correct errors that were not discovered during the product development phases
Perfective Maintenance
docs.text:
• Improve implementation of the system
  • Enhance functionalities of the system

docs.title: Adaptive Maintenance
docs.text:
• Port software to a new environment
  • eg: to a new computer or to a new OS

docs.title: 📘 Definition
docs.text:
Prewritten software available for purchase.

That means:

  • It is already developed.

  • It is not built for one specific customer.

  • Anyone can buy and use it.

This falls under Product-based software.

docs.title: 🔍 Key Characteristics
docs.text:
• Developed for the general market

  • Same version used by many users

  • Sold via license or subscription

  • Company decides features

  • User adapts to software

docs.title: 🧠 Simple Example
docs.text:
Suppose you buy:

  • Windows

  • MS Office

  • Antivirus software

You don’t tell Microsoft:

“Add this feature for me.”

You buy what is already available.

That is packaged software.

docs.title: 🎯 Why “Packaged”?
docs.text:
Because it’s like a ready-made product in a box.

Like buying:

  • A calculator

  • A microwave

  • A textbook

You don’t customize it — you use it as it is.

docs.title: 📘 Definition (based on your PDF)
docs.text:
Software developed at some user’s request. Usually developer tailors some generic solution.

This means:

  • Built for a specific client

  • Designed according to client requirements

  • Not sold to the general public

This falls under Service-based software.

docs.title: 🔍 Key Characteristics
docs.text:
• Client-specific

  • Requirements defined by client

  • May reuse existing frameworks

  • Often owned by client

  • Paid through contract

docs.title: 🧠 Example
docs.text:
A hospital wants:

  • Patient record system

  • Billing system

  • Appointment system

A company develops it specifically for that hospital.

Other hospitals cannot buy it directly.

That is custom software.

docs.title: 🔥 Core Difference (Very Important)
docs.text: Aspect Packaged Software Custom Software Built For Mass market Specific client Requirements Defined by company Defined by client Ownership Company Often client Modification Limited Fully customizable Cost per User Lower Higher Risk Market risk Contract risk

docs.title: 🔹 3️⃣ Vertical Market Software
docs.text: This term appears in your PDF.

docs.title: 📘 Definition
docs.text:
Designed for a particular industry.

It is still packaged software, but targeted.

docs.title: 🔍 Example
docs.text:
Software built only for:

  • Hospitals

  • Banks

  • Airlines

  • Insurance companies

For example:

  • A banking core system sold to many banks

It is not for general users. It is specific to one industry.

That is vertical market software.

docs.title: 📘 Definition
docs.text:
Meets needs of many companies across industries.

These are general-purpose tools.

docs.title: 🔍 Example
docs.text:
• MS Excel

  • Word processors

  • Email software

  • Database systems

Used in:

  • Hospitals

  • Banks

  • Schools

  • Corporates

Same product, different industries.

That is horizontal software.

docs.title: 🧩 Full Classification (Clear Structure)
docs.text:
Software Types:

1️⃣ Packaged Software   • Horizontal Market   • Vertical Market

2️⃣ Custom Software

docs.title: 🎯 Real-World Analogy
docs.text:
Imagine clothes:

  • Packaged software = Ready-made clothes

  • Custom software = Tailor-stitched clothes

  • Vertical = School uniform (specific sector)

  • Horizontal = Jeans (used everywhere)

docs.title: 🧠 Why This Distinction Matters in Software Engineering
docs.text:
Because:

  • Development approach differs

  • Risk management differs

  • Cost estimation differs

  • Maintenance strategy differs

  • Business model differs

Packaged software needs:

  • Market research

  • Version updates

  • Competition strategy

Custom software needs:

  • Requirement clarity

  • Client communication

  • Contract management

docs.title: 💡 One Very Important Concept from PDF
docs.text:
Your slides mention:

Nowadays, many projects are services — meaning customization and reuse.

Modern development:

  • Rarely builds everything from scratch

  • Often modifies existing software

  • Uses reusable libraries

So the line between packaged and custom is sometimes blurred.

docs.title: Packaged Software
docs.text: Prewritten, sold to many users.

docs.title: Custom Software
docs.text: Built specifically for one client.

docs.title: Vertical Market
docs.text: Industry-specific packaged software.

docs.title: Horizontal Market
docs.text: General-purpose packaged software.

docs.title: 🟢 What is a Software Product?
docs.text:
A software product is:

Generic software developed for a large number of users and sold in the open market.

It is not built for one specific customer.

docs.title: Key Characteristics:
docs.text:
• Built for mass market

  • Same version sold to many users

  • Developer decides features

  • Revenue comes from selling licenses/subscriptions

  • High initial investment

docs.title: Example:
docs.text:
• Windows OS

  • MS Office

  • Photoshop

  • Antivirus software

These are product-based companies.

docs.title: Important:
docs.text:
The company owns:

  • Intellectual property

  • Source code

  • Branding

  • Future roadmap

docs.title: 🔵 What is a Software Service?
docs.text:
A software service is:

Software developed or customized for a specific client according to their requirements.

It is built on request.

docs.title: Key Characteristics:
docs.text:
• Built for a specific client

  • Client defines requirements

  • Revenue from contract/payment

  • Often involves customization

  • Intellectual property may belong to client

docs.title: Includes:
docs.text:
• Custom software development

  • Maintenance

  • Testing services

  • Contract programming

docs.title: 🔥 Real Difference (Core Understanding)
docs.text:
Let’s compare deeply:

Aspect Product Service Target Users Many customers One specific client Requirements Decided by company Decided by client Risk High (market risk) Lower (client pays) Investment Company invests first Client funds development Ownership Company owns IP Often client owns Revenue Model Sales/subscription Contract billing Examples Windows, Oracle DB Custom ERP for hospital

docs.title: 💡 Simple Analogy
docs.text:
Think of it like this:

Product = Ready-made shirt sold in store Service = Tailor stitching shirt for you

One is mass-produced. Other is customized.

docs.title: 🚀 Why India Focused on Services?
docs.text:
Service model:

  • Lower business risk

  • Less capital investment

  • Faster revenue

  • High demand globally

That’s why companies like TCS, Infosys, Wipro focused heavily on services.

docs.title: Product vs Service:
docs.text:
• Product = Generic, market-based

  • Service = Client-specific, contract-based

docs.text:
• Requirements Gathering
    • understand the users requirements
