docs.title: Software Lifecycle
docs.text: A Software Life Cycle represents the journey of a software product from the moment someone thinks of it until it is no longer used. To manage this journey effectively, engineers use Life Cycle Models (also called SDLC or Process Models), which are descriptive and diagrammatic plans that tell a team exactly what to do and when to do it.

docs.title: 1. What is a Software Life Cycle?
docs.text: The software life cycle is a series of identifiable stages that a software product undergoes during its lifetime. These stages ensure that the software is built systematically rather than by "guessing".

docs.title: The Core Phases
docs.text:
Most models include these basic steps:

  1. Feasibility Study: Deciding if the project is financially and technically possible.
  2. Requirements Analysis and Specification: Talking to the customer to understand exactly what they need and writing it down in a Software Requirements Specification (SRS) document.
  3. Design: Creating a blueprint of the software’s structure, data, and algorithms.
  4. Coding and Unit Testing: Writing the actual code and testing small pieces (modules) independently.
  5. Integration and System Testing: Putting all pieces together and checking if the whole system meets the customer's requirements.
  6. Maintenance: The longest phase, where bugs are fixed and new features are added after the software is released.

docs.title: 2. Why Use a Life Cycle Model?
docs.text:
Without a model, team members might start different tasks at the wrong time—for example, one person coding while another is still trying to figure out the requirements—which leads to chaos and project failure.

  • Milestones: Models provide "checkpoints" (like phase entry and exit criteria) that help managers track progress.
  • The 99% Complete Syndrome: Without a model, developers often guess their progress, leading to the problem where a project stays "99% finished" for months because no one knows exactly what is left to do.

docs.title: I. The Classical Waterfall Model
docs.text:
This is the oldest, simplest, and most intuitive model. It views development as a steady downward flow, like a waterfall, where you must finish one phase before starting the next.

  • Best for: Projects where requirements are very stable and well-understood.
  • Weakness: It is idealistic and assumes no mistakes are made, making it hard to go back and fix errors found later.

docs.title: II. The Iterative Waterfall Model
docs.text:
Since the classical model is too perfect for the real world, the Iterative Waterfall Model adds "feedback paths".

  • Concept: It recognizes that errors are introduced in every phase and allows you to go back to a previous phase to fix them.
  • Phase Containment: It emphasizes catching errors in the same phase they were made to keep costs low.

docs.title: III. The V-Model (Verification and Validation)
docs.text:
This model is a variant of the waterfall that emphasizes testing.

  • The "V" Shape: For every development phase (like Design), there is a corresponding testing phase (like Integration Testing) planned at the same time.
  • Example: While you are writing the Requirements, you also write the plan for the final System Test.

docs.title: IV. The Prototyping Model
docs.text:
Before building the real system, developers build a Prototype—a "toy" version with limited features.

  • Why? It helps customers "see" the software early so they can clarify what they actually want.
  • The "Throw-away" rule: Usually, the prototype's code is messy and is thrown away once the requirements are clear.

docs.title: V. Evolutionary & Incremental Models
docs.text:
Instead of delivering the whole software at once, these models deliver it in pieces called Increments.

  • Evolutionary: You build the core modules first and then refine them over many versions based on user feedback.
  • Advantage: Users get to see and use parts of the system much earlier than with a waterfall approach.

docs.title: VI. The Spiral Model (Meta-Model)
docs.text:
The Spiral Model is a high-end model that focuses heavily on Risk Analysis.

  • Quadrants: Each loop of the spiral involves identifying objectives, analyzing risks, developing a version, and planning the next step.
  • Example: If there is a risk that a new technology won't work, the spiral model will force the team to build a prototype specifically to test that technology first.

docs.title: VII. RAD (Rapid Application Development)
docs.text:
RAD is designed to build software very fast and at a low cost.

  • Technique: It relies on making short-term plans (called Time Boxes) and heavily reusing existing code.
  • Trade-off: It is fast, but the final quality and documentation might be lower than other models.

docs.title: VIII. Agile Models (e.g., Scrum and XP)
docs.text:
Agile is the modern standard for software that changes frequently.

  • Core Idea: It values people and working software over long plans and heavy documentation.
  • Scrum: Work is done in month-long iterations called Sprints.
  • Extreme Programming (XP): Takes "best practices" to the extreme, such as Pair Programming (two people coding at one machine) and Test-Driven Development.

docs.title: IX. The Unified Process (RUP)
docs.text:
Developed by Booch, Jacobson, and Rumbaugh, this is a large, professional framework that is both incremental and iterative.

  • Four Phases: It organizes work into Inception, Elaboration, Construction, and Transition.
  • Visualizing Progress: It uses two dimensions—one for time (phases) and one for core activities (like modeling and implementation).

docs.title: Software Engineering - Midsem Exam Answers (Part 1)
docs.text: Based on the textbook "Object-Oriented Software Engineering: Practical Software Development using UML and Java" by Timothy C. Lethbridge and Robert Laganière

docs.title: Short Answer Questions
docs.text:
Q1. Define Software Engineering. What makes it different from programming?

Answer: Software Engineering is the process of solving customers' problems by the systematic development and evolution of large, high-quality software systems within cost, time and other constraints.

Difference from programming: - Programming is just one activity of software engineering (implementation) - Software engineering includes requirements gathering, design, implementation, verification, and maintenance - Software engineering focuses on solving customer problems, not just writing code - Software engineering involves systematic, disciplined approaches rather than ad-hoc coding

Q2. List and briefly explain the four main activities of software engineering.

Answer: 1. Requirements Gathering: Understanding and documenting what the customer needs 2. Design: Creating a plan for how the software will be built (architecture, detailed design) 3. Implementation: Writing the actual code based on the design 4. Verification and Validation: Testing to ensure the software meets requirements and works correctly

Q3. What are the three main types of software systems? Give one example of each.

Answer: 1. Custom software: Developed specifically for one customer (e.g., a bank's internal trading system) 2. Generic (off-the-shelf) software: Sold to multiple customers (e.g., Microsoft Office) 3. Embedded software: Built into hardware devices (e.g., software in a microwave oven)

Q4. Explain the difference between a customer and a user in software engineering context.

Answer: - Customer: The person or organization who pays for the software. They decide what features are needed and approve the budget. - User: The person who actually uses the software to perform their work. They may have different needs than the customer. - Sometimes they are the same person, but often not. Understanding both is crucial for success.

Q5. What is the 80-20 rule (Pareto Principle) and how does it apply to software engineering?

Answer: The 80-20 rule states that 80% of the value to the customer is delivered with 20% of the work.

Application to SE: - Focus on the most important features first - In iterative development, deliver the most valuable 20% of features in early iterations - Helps prioritize requirements and manage scope - Explains why incremental development is effective

docs.title: Long Answer Questions
docs.text:
Q6. Discuss the importance of understanding the customer and user in software engineering. What techniques can be used to gather information about their needs?

Answer: Importance: - Software exists to solve customer problems - without understanding them, we build the wrong thing - Users must be able to work efficiently with the software - Poor understanding leads to project failure, unused software, endless change requests - Ensures both utility (solves the problem) and usability (easy to use)

Techniques for gathering information: 1. Interviews: One-on-one discussions with stakeholders 2. Brainstorming: Group sessions to generate ideas 3. Use case analysis: Understanding how users will interact with the system 4. Prototyping: Creating mock-ups to get feedback 5. Domain analysis: Studying the business domain and existing systems 6. Observation: Watching users work with current systems 7. Questionnaires: Surveys for large user groups

Q7. Explain why software engineering is considered a labor-intensive activity. What are the implications of this for project management?

Answer: Why labor-intensive: - Software is built by people writing code, not by machines - Requires skilled professionals (software engineers) - Much of the work is creative and intellectual - Automation is limited compared to manufacturing

Implications for project management: - Need for effective team communication and coordination - Importance of training and skill development - Difficulty in measuring progress (can't just count widgets) - Need for good cost estimation techniques - Importance of team structure and organization - Risk of personnel shortfalls - Communication overhead increases with team size

Q8. Describe the nine themes that are incorporated throughout the textbook for effective software engineering.

Answer: 1. Understanding the customer and user: Focus on solving their problems 2. Basing development on solid principles and reusable technology: Apply well-understood knowledge 3. Object orientation: Use abstraction, inheritance, polymorphism 4. Visual modeling using UML: Communicate designs effectively 5. Evaluation of alternatives in requirements and design: Make informed decisions 6. Incorporating quantitative and logical thinking: Use metrics and formal methods 7. Iterative and agile development: Deliver in small increments 8. Communicating effectively using documentation: Keep stakeholders informed 9. Risk management in all software engineering activities: Identify and mitigate risks

docs.title: 2. EVOLUTION OF SOFTWARE ENGINEERING TECHNIQUES - ANSWERS
Short Answer Questions
docs.text:
Q1. What was the "software crisis" that led to the development of software engineering as a discipline?

Answer: The software crisis occurred in the 1960s-1970s when: - Software projects were consistently over budget and behind schedule - Software quality was poor with many defects - Software often failed to meet user needs - Maintenance was extremely difficult - Projects were becoming larger and more complex

This led to the recognition that software development needed systematic, engineering-like approaches rather than ad-hoc programming.

Q2. How has the focus of software engineering evolved from the 1960s to the present day?

Answer: - 1960s-1970s: Focus on coding, structured programming - 1980s: Focus on design, structured analysis and design - 1990s: Rise of object-orientation, UML, process models - 2000s-present: Agile methods, iterative development, emphasis on people and communication, DevOps

The evolution moved from code-centric to process-centric to people-centric approaches.

Q3. What is the difference between structured programming and object-oriented programming?

Answer: | Aspect | Structured Programming | Object-Oriented Programming | |--------|----------------------|----------------------------| | Focus | Procedures/functions | Objects that contain data and behavior | | Data | Separate from functions | Encapsulated with functions | | Reuse | Limited | High through inheritance | | Modularity | Functions | Classes | | Communication | Function calls | Message passing |

Q4. Explain the shift from waterfall to iterative/agile approaches in software development.

Answer: Reasons for shift: - Waterfall assumes requirements are fully understood upfront - rarely true - Changes are expensive in waterfall - Customers want to see progress early - Risk is not addressed until late in waterfall - Iterative approaches allow learning and adaptation

Benefits of iterative/agile: - Early delivery of working software - Better handling of changing requirements - Reduced risk through early feedback - Customer satisfaction through involvement - Continuous improvement

docs.title: Long Answer Questions
docs.text:
Q5. Trace the evolution of software development methodologies from the early days to modern agile approaches. What factors drove these changes?

Answer: Evolution:

  1. 1950s-1960s: Opportunistic Approach
  2. Ad-hoc coding without systematic process

  3. Problems: Poor quality, unmaintainable code

  4. 1970s: Structured Programming

  5. Focus on clear control structures
  6. Top-down design

  7. Still code-centric

  8. 1980s: Structured Analysis and Design

  9. Data flow diagrams
  10. Entity-relationship diagrams

  11. Separation of analysis and design

  12. 1990s: Object-Oriented Methods

  13. OOP languages (C++, Java)
  14. UML for modeling

  15. Unified Process

  16. 2000s-present: Agile Methods

  17. XP, Scrum, etc.
  18. Lightweight processes
  19. Focus on people over processes

Driving factors: - Increasing software complexity - Need for faster delivery - Changing requirements - Recognition that people are key - Desire for better quality - Cost pressures

Q6. Discuss how the introduction of UML changed software engineering practices. What problems did it solve?

Answer: UML Introduction: - Unified Modeling Language standardized in 1997 - Combined best of multiple OO modeling notations

Problems it solved: 1. Inconsistent notations: Before UML, many competing notations (Booch, OMT, OOSE) 2. Communication: Provided common visual language for teams 3. Documentation: Standard way to document designs 4. Tool support: Enabled CASE tools 5. Abstraction: Helped think at higher level than code

Impact: - Became industry standard for OO modeling - Essential for design communication - Foundation for model-driven development

Q7. Compare and contrast the traditional "opportunistic approach" with modern software engineering practices. What are the problems with the opportunistic approach?

Answer: Opportunistic Approach: - Start coding immediately without analysis or design - Fix problems as they arise - No systematic process

Problems: 1. Requirements not understood → wrong system built 2. No design → poor architecture, hard to maintain 3. No testing plan → many defects discovered late 4. No documentation → knowledge lost 5. No project management → over budget, late delivery 6. Poor quality → customer dissatisfaction

Modern SE Practices: - Systematic requirements gathering - Design before coding - Planned testing - Documentation - Project management - Quality assurance throughout

docs.title: Short Answer Questions
docs.text:
Q1. List the phases of the Software Development Life Cycle (SDLC) in their typical order.

Answer: 1. Requirements Gathering and Analysis 2. System Design 3. Implementation (Coding) 4. Testing (Verification and Validation) 5. Deployment 6. Maintenance

Q2. What is the purpose of the requirements gathering phase in SDLC?

Answer: - Understand what the customer needs - Document functional and non-functional requirements - Define system scope - Establish acceptance criteria - Create basis for design and testing - Get stakeholder agreement

Q3. Why is the maintenance phase considered the most expensive phase of the SDLC?

Answer: - Software typically remains in use for many years - Maintenance includes: - Corrective maintenance (fixing bugs) - Adaptive maintenance (adapting to new environments) - Perfective maintenance (adding new features) - Preventive maintenance (improving quality) - Studies show maintenance can cost 60-80% of total lifecycle cost - Poor initial design makes maintenance more expensive

Q4. What is verification and validation (V&V) and when is it performed in the SDLC?

Answer: - Verification: "Are we building the product right?" - checking that the software meets its specification - Validation: "Are we building the right product?" - checking that the software meets user needs

When performed: - Throughout the SDLC, not just at the end - Requirements review (validation) - Design review (verification) - Code review (verification) - Testing (both verification and validation) - Acceptance testing (validation)

docs.title: Long Answer Questions
docs.text:
Q5. Describe the complete Software Development Life Cycle. Explain what activities are performed in each phase and how they relate to each other.

Answer: 1. Requirements Gathering and Analysis: - Activities: Interview stakeholders, analyze domain, document requirements, create use cases - Output: Software Requirements Specification (SRS)

2. System Design: - Activities: Architectural design, detailed design, database design, interface design - Output: Design documents, UML diagrams

3. Implementation: - Activities: Coding, unit testing, code review - Output: Source code, unit test results

4. Testing: - Activities: Integration testing, system testing, acceptance testing - Output: Test reports, defect reports

5. Deployment: - Activities: Installation, data migration, user training - Output: Deployed system, documentation

6. Maintenance: - Activities: Bug fixes, enhancements, adaptations - Output: Updated system

Relationships: - Each phase builds on the previous - Feedback loops allow going back to earlier phases - Traceability links requirements through to code and tests

Q6. Explain the concept of traceability in the context of SDLC. Why is it important?

Answer: Traceability is the ability to follow the life of a requirement from its origin through implementation and testing.

Types: - Forward traceability: Requirements → Design → Code → Tests - Backward traceability: Tests → Code → Design → Requirements - Bidirectional traceability: Both directions

Importance: 1. Impact analysis: When requirements change, know what needs to be modified 2. Verification: Ensure all requirements are implemented 3. Testing: Ensure all requirements are tested 4. Maintenance: Understand why code exists 5. Compliance: Meet regulatory requirements 6. Project management: Track progress against requirements

Q7. Discuss why requirements changes are inevitable in software development. How should a software engineer handle these changes throughout the SDLC?

Answer: Why changes are inevitable: - Customers learn more as they see the system - Business environment changes - Technology changes - New stakeholders emerge - Initial requirements were incomplete or incorrect - Competitive pressures

Handling changes: 1. Expect changes: Plan for them from the start 2. Iterative development: Deliver in increments to get early feedback 3. Change control process: - Document change requests - Analyze impact (cost, schedule, quality) - Get approval from stakeholders - Implement approved changes 4. Traceability: Maintain links to assess impact 5. Configuration management: Track all versions 6. Communication: Keep all stakeholders informed 7. Prioritization: Focus on most valuable changes

docs.title: Waterfall Model
docs.text:
Q1. Draw and label the waterfall model. List its phases in order.

Answer:

┌─────────────────┐
│   Requirements  │
└────────┬────────┘
         ▼
┌─────────────────┐
│      Design     │
└────────┬────────┘
         ▼
┌─────────────────┐
│  Implementation │
└────────┬────────┘
         ▼
┌─────────────────┐
│  Verification   │
└────────┬────────┘
         ▼
┌─────────────────┐
│   Maintenance   │
└─────────────────┘

Phases: Requirements → Design → Implementation → Verification → Maintenance

Q2. What are the main limitations of the waterfall model?

Answer: 1. Requirements must be complete before design starts - rarely possible 2. No working software until late in the process 3. High risk - problems discovered late 4. Difficult to accommodate changes 5. No customer feedback during development 6. Assumes phases don't overlap 7. Not suitable for complex or innovative projects

Q3. When is the waterfall model most appropriate?

Answer: - Requirements are well-understood and unlikely to change - System is similar to previous systems - Technical challenges are well-understood - Short project with clear deliverables - Regulatory environment requires complete documentation upfront - Example: Porting an existing system to a new platform

docs.title: Iterative Waterfall Model
docs.text:
Q4. How does the iterative waterfall model differ from the pure waterfall model?

Answer: The iterative waterfall model allows feedback loops between phases: - Can go back from design to requirements if issues found - Can go back from implementation to design - Can go back from testing to implementation

This makes it more flexible than the pure sequential waterfall.

Q5. What is the advantage of allowing feedback loops between phases in the iterative waterfall model?

Answer: - Problems discovered in later phases can be fixed by going back - Reduces risk of building the wrong system - Allows for some requirements refinement - More realistic than pure waterfall - Still maintains overall sequential structure

docs.title: Prototyping Model
docs.text:
Q6. What is a prototype in software development? What are the two types of prototypes?

Answer: A prototype is a preliminary version of the system used to explore requirements or design options.

Two types: 1. Throwaway (disposable) prototype: Built quickly to learn, then discarded 2. Evolutionary prototype: Built and refined into the final system

Q7. What is the main purpose of prototyping?

Answer: - Explore requirements when they're not well understood - Get early feedback from users - Reduce risk of building the wrong system - Validate design approaches - Demonstrate feasibility - Help users articulate needs they couldn't express verbally

Q8. Explain the difference between throwaway prototyping and evolutionary prototyping.

Answer:

Aspect Throwaway Evolutionary Purpose Learn and discard Build upon Quality Quick and dirty Production quality Code Discarded Kept and refined Risk Lower (no commitment) Higher (foundation for system) When used Early requirements Throughout development

docs.title: Incremental Model
docs.text:
Q9. What is incremental development? How does it differ from the waterfall model?

Answer: Incremental development delivers the system in small, usable increments (pieces).

Differences from waterfall:

Waterfall Incremental Deliver all at once Deliver in parts One big release Multiple small releases Late feedback Early and continuous feedback High risk Lower risk Difficult to change Easier to accommodate changes

Q10. What are the advantages of the incremental model?

Answer: 1. Early delivery of working software 2. Customer gets value sooner 3. Feedback from early increments improves later ones 4. Lower risk - problems found early 5. Easier to manage changes 6. Better resource utilization 7. If project fails, something is still delivered

docs.title: V-Model
docs.text:
Q11. Draw the V-model and explain its structure.

Answer:

        Requirements
           /\
          /  \
         /    \
    System    System
    Design    Testing
       /\      /\
      /  \    /  \
     /    \  /    \
  Module  Integration
  Design    Testing
     /\      /\
    /  \    /  \
   /    \  /    \
Coding  Unit Testing

Structure: - Left side (descending): Development activities (requirements → design → coding) - Right side (ascending): Testing activities (unit → integration → system) - Each development phase has a corresponding testing phase

Q12. What is the relationship between the left side and right side of the V-model?

Answer: - Each level on the left has a corresponding test level on the right - Requirements ↔ System Testing - System Design ↔ Integration Testing - Module Design ↔ Unit Testing - The V-model emphasizes that testing should be planned from the start - Test plans are created during the corresponding development phase

docs.title: Evolutionary/Spiral Model
docs.text:
Q13. Who developed the spiral model? What are its four quadrants?

Answer: The spiral model was developed by Barry Boehm in 1988.

Four quadrants: 1. Determine objectives, alternatives, constraints 2. Evaluate alternatives, identify and resolve risks 3. Develop and verify next-level product 4. Plan the next iteration

Q14. What is risk analysis and why is it important in the spiral model?

Answer: Risk analysis is the process of identifying potential problems that could affect the project and determining how to address them.

Importance in spiral model: - Risk analysis is explicit in every iteration - Highest risks are addressed first - Helps decide whether to proceed with the project - Reduces overall project risk - Makes risk management a core activity

Q15. Explain Fred Brooks' famous quotation about building a throwaway system.

Answer: Quote: "The question is not whether to build a pilot system and throw it away. You will do that. The question is whether to plan in advance to build a throwaway."

Meaning: - First attempts at building software are often learning experiences - The first version often needs to be discarded - Better to plan for this and build a throwaway prototype deliberately - This reduces risk and improves the final system - Supports the evolutionary approach

docs.title: Long Answer Questions
docs.text:
Q16. Compare and contrast the Waterfall model and the Spiral model. What are the advantages and disadvantages of each? When would you use one over the other?

Answer:

Aspect Waterfall Spiral Approach Sequential Iterative with risk focus Risk handling Implicit, late Explicit, early Flexibility Low High Customer feedback Late Continuous Documentation Heavy Moderate Cost visibility Late Early

Waterfall - Advantages: - Simple to understand - Clear milestones - Good for well-understood projects - Complete documentation

Waterfall - Disadvantages: - Inflexible - Late problem discovery - No early working software - Poor for complex projects

Spiral - Advantages: - Risk-driven - Early problem detection - Flexible - Good for large, complex projects

Spiral - Disadvantages: - Complex to manage - Can be expensive - Requires risk analysis expertise - May not be suitable for small projects

When to use: - Waterfall: Small, well-understood projects; regulatory requirements - Spiral: Large, complex, high-risk projects; innovative systems

Q17. Explain the Phased-Release model. How does it address some of the problems of the waterfall model?

Answer: Phased-Release Model: - System is divided into releases - Each release goes through complete waterfall phases - Releases are delivered sequentially - Later releases add more functionality

Addressing waterfall problems: 1. Late delivery: Working software delivered after first release 2. No feedback: Customer sees and uses early releases 3. High risk: Risk reduced by delivering in parts 4. Changes difficult: Changes can be incorporated in later releases 5. All-or-nothing: If project fails, earlier releases still delivered

Q18. Describe the Evolutionary model. What does it show that is not clear from the spiral model?

Answer: Evolutionary Model: - System evolves through multiple versions - Each version is a complete, usable system - Versions progressively add functionality - Early versions may be prototypes

What it shows that spiral doesn't: - The spiral model shows the process but not the system evolution - Evolutionary model explicitly shows how the system grows - Shows that early versions can be deployed - Emphasizes that the system is always in a deliverable state - Shows the progressive nature of development

Q19. Discuss the Concurrent Engineering model. How does it account for the "divide and conquer" principle?

Answer: Concurrent Engineering Model: - Multiple activities happen in parallel - Different teams work on different aspects simultaneously - Not strictly sequential like waterfall

Divide and conquer: - System divided into subsystems - Different teams work on different subsystems concurrently - Integration happens when subsystems are complete - Reduces overall project time - Allows specialization

Example: - UI team works on interface - Database team works on data layer - Business logic team works on core functionality - All happen at the same time

Q20. What is eXtreme Programming (XP)? List and explain at least five of its key tenets.

Answer: eXtreme Programming (XP) is an agile methodology that emphasizes customer satisfaction through rapid delivery of useful software.

Key tenets:

  1. Incremental planning: Requirements recorded on story cards; frequent releases
  2. Small releases: Develop small, incremental releases to get rapid feedback
  3. Simple design: Do the simplest thing that could possibly work
  4. Test-first development: Write tests before writing code
  5. Refactoring: Continuously improve code structure
  6. Pair programming: Two programmers work together at one machine
  7. Collective ownership: Anyone can change any code
  8. Continuous integration: Integrate and build frequently
  9. On-site customer: Customer is part of the team
  10. Sustainable pace: Work at a pace that can be sustained indefinitely

Q21. Compare the Agile approach with traditional process models. What are the advantages and drawbacks of agile methods?

Answer:

Aspect Traditional (Waterfall) Agile Process Heavy, prescriptive Light, adaptive Documentation Extensive Minimal, just enough Planning Upfront Continuous Changes Discouraged Embraced Customer involvement At milestones Continuous Team structure Hierarchical Self-organizing

Agile - Advantages: - Responds to change quickly - Customer satisfaction through early delivery - Working software is primary measure of progress - Face-to-face communication - Technical excellence - Simplicity

Agile - Drawbacks: - Can be difficult to scale to large projects - Requires experienced team members - Less documentation may cause problems later - Customer availability required - Hard to estimate costs upfront - May not suit all project types

Q22. Explain how you would choose a process model for a particular project. What factors would you consider?

Answer: Factors to consider:

  1. Requirements clarity:
  2. Well-understood → Waterfall

  3. Unclear → Prototyping, Spiral, Agile

  4. Project size:

  5. Small → Any model

  6. Large → Spiral, Phased-Release

  7. Risk level:

  8. Low → Waterfall, Incremental

  9. High → Spiral, Prototyping

  10. Customer availability:

  11. Available → Agile

  12. Limited → Waterfall

  13. Team experience:

  14. Experienced → Agile

  15. Novice → Waterfall with guidance

  16. Technology familiarity:

  17. Known → Waterfall

  18. New → Prototyping, Spiral

  19. Regulatory requirements:

  20. Strict documentation → Waterfall

  21. Flexible → Agile

  22. Time to market:

  23. Critical → Incremental, Agile
  24. Flexible → Waterfall

docs.title: Short Answer Questions
docs.text:
Q1. What is a feasibility study? What are its main objectives?

Answer: A feasibility study is an analysis that determines whether a proposed project is viable and worth pursuing.

Objectives: 1. Determine if the project is technically possible 2. Assess if the project is economically justified 3. Check if the project can be completed within constraints 4. Identify potential risks 5. Provide basis for go/no-go decision

Q2. List the three main types of feasibility that should be considered.

Answer: 1. Technical feasibility: Can it be built with available technology? 2. Economic feasibility: Is it cost-effective? Will benefits exceed costs? 3. Schedule feasibility: Can it be completed within the required timeframe?

Q3. What is technical feasibility? Give an example of a project that might be technically infeasible.

Answer: Technical feasibility assesses whether the proposed system can be developed with available technology, expertise, and resources.

Example of technically infeasible project: - A real-time translation system in 1980s (before adequate speech recognition existed) - A system requiring more processing power than available - A system requiring integration with incompatible legacy systems without interfaces

Q4. What is economic feasibility? How is it determined?

Answer: Economic feasibility assesses whether the project is financially viable.

Determined by: - Cost-benefit analysis - Calculating total cost of ownership (development + maintenance) - Estimating benefits (tangible and intangible) - Computing return on investment (ROI) - Break-even analysis

If benefits exceed costs, the project is economically feasible.

Q5. What is schedule feasibility?

Answer: Schedule feasibility assesses whether the project can be completed within the required timeframe.

Considerations: - Available resources (people, equipment) - Task dependencies - Critical path analysis - Risk factors that could cause delays - Market window (when product is needed)

docs.title: Long Answer Questions
docs.text:
Q6. Describe the components of a feasibility study. What should be included in a feasibility study report?

Answer: Components of feasibility study:

  1. Technical feasibility analysis:
  2. Technology assessment
  3. Technical risk evaluation

  4. Resource availability

  5. Economic feasibility analysis:

  6. Cost estimation
  7. Benefit analysis

  8. ROI calculation

  9. Schedule feasibility analysis:

  10. Timeline assessment
  11. Resource scheduling

  12. Critical path identification

  13. Operational feasibility:

  14. Will the system be used?

  15. Will it solve the business problem?

  16. Legal/feasibility:

  17. Regulatory compliance
  18. Intellectual property issues

Feasibility study report contents: - Executive summary - Project description - Analysis of each feasibility type - Risk assessment - Recommendations - Appendices with detailed calculations

Q7. Explain how you would conduct a feasibility study for a proposed software system. What steps would you follow?

Answer: Steps:

  1. Understand the proposed system:
  2. Review requirements

  3. Understand scope

  4. Assess technical feasibility:

  5. Identify required technology
  6. Evaluate team's technical capability

  7. Identify technical risks

  8. Assess economic feasibility:

  9. Estimate development costs
  10. Estimate maintenance costs
  11. Estimate benefits

  12. Perform cost-benefit analysis

  13. Assess schedule feasibility:

  14. Break down into tasks
  15. Estimate task durations
  16. Identify dependencies

  17. Create preliminary schedule

  18. Identify risks:

  19. List potential problems
  20. Assess probability and impact

  21. Develop mitigation strategies

  22. Prepare report:

  23. Document findings
  24. Make recommendation
  25. Present to stakeholders

Q8. Discuss the importance of feasibility study in the software development process. What happens if a feasibility study is not conducted properly?

Answer: Importance: - Prevents investment in unviable projects - Identifies risks early - Provides basis for decision making - Helps set realistic expectations - Can save significant costs - Ensures alignment with business goals

Consequences of poor feasibility study: 1. Project failure: Discovering infeasibility after significant investment 2. Cost overruns: Underestimating costs 3. Schedule delays: Unrealistic timelines 4. Technical problems: Using inappropriate technology 5. Abandoned projects: Wasted resources 6. Damaged reputation: Failed projects affect organization credibility 7. Missed opportunities: Resources tied up in unviable projects

Continue to Part 2 for Requirement Analysis, SRS, Requirement Modeling, and Use Case Diagrams

docs.title: Short Answer Questions
docs.text:
Q1. What is requirement analysis? Why is it important?

Answer: Requirement analysis is the process of understanding, documenting, and validating what the customer needs from the software system.

Importance: - Foundation for all subsequent development activities - Ensures the right system is built - Reduces risk of project failure - Provides basis for testing - Helps manage scope - Enables accurate cost and schedule estimation - Poor requirements are a leading cause of project failure

Q2. List four techniques for gathering requirements.

Answer: 1. Interviews - One-on-one discussions with stakeholders 2. Brainstorming - Group sessions to generate ideas 3. Use case analysis - Understanding user interactions 4. Prototyping - Creating mock-ups for feedback 5. Observation - Watching users work 6. Questionnaires - Surveys for large groups 7. Document analysis - Studying existing documentation

Q3. What is domain analysis? Why should it be performed before gathering requirements?

Answer: Domain analysis is the study of the business domain to understand terminology, processes, and existing systems.

Why perform first: - Ensures effective communication with stakeholders - Prevents misunderstandings - Helps ask better questions - Understands existing solutions - Identifies constraints - Builds credibility with domain experts - Avoids reinventing the wheel

Q4. What is the difference between functional and non-functional requirements? Give two examples of each.

Answer:

Functional Requirements Non-Functional Requirements Describe WHAT the system should do Describe HOW the system should behave Define specific behaviors Define quality attributes

Examples of functional requirements: 1. The system shall allow users to search for products by name 2. The system shall send an email confirmation after order placement

Examples of non-functional requirements: 1. The system shall respond to user queries within 2 seconds 2. The system shall be available 99.9% of the time

Q5. What are quality requirements? Give three examples.

Answer: Quality requirements (also called non-functional requirements) specify the quality attributes the system must have.

Examples: 1. Performance: System shall process 100 transactions per second 2. Reliability: System shall have 99.9% uptime 3. Usability: New users shall learn the system within 2 hours 4. Security: All data shall be encrypted 5. Maintainability: Code shall have cyclomatic complexity less than 10

Q6. What is the difference between a feature and a requirement?

Answer:

Feature Requirement High-level capability Detailed specification "The system shall have online payment" "The system shall process credit card payments through Visa and MasterCard" Often marketing-oriented Technical specification May include multiple requirements Single, verifiable statement

Q7. What is gold-plating? Why should it be avoided?

Answer: Gold-plating is adding features that are not necessary to solve the customer's problem.

Why avoid it: - Increases cost without adding value - Extends schedule - Adds complexity - Increases maintenance burden - May introduce defects - Diverts resources from important features - Principle: "Build only what is needed"

docs.title: Long Answer Questions
docs.text:
Q8. Describe the process of requirements gathering. What techniques can be used and when is each most appropriate?

Answer: Process: 1. Identify stakeholders 2. Understand the domain 3. Select appropriate techniques 4. Gather information 5. Document findings 6. Validate with stakeholders 7. Iterate as needed

Techniques and when to use:

Technique When to Use Interviews Small number of key stakeholders; detailed understanding needed Brainstorming Early stage; generating ideas; creative solutions Use case analysis Understanding user interactions; functional requirements Prototyping Requirements unclear; UI design; getting user feedback Observation Users can't articulate needs; understanding actual work Questionnaires Large user groups; quantitative data needed Document analysis Existing systems; regulatory requirements

Q9. Explain the principles for gathering good requirements as discussed in the textbook.

Answer: 1. Perform domain analysis - Know enough to communicate effectively 2. Keep scope narrow - Focus on the real problem 3. Keep system general - Find higher-level goals 4. Gather all types - Functional, quality, platform, process 5. Combine techniques - Use multiple approaches for best results 6. Involve users - They know their needs best 7. Iterate - Requirements evolve 8. Document clearly - Unambiguous, verifiable 9. Validate - Get stakeholder agreement 10. Prioritize - Not all requirements are equal

Q10. Discuss the different types of requirements (functional, quality, platform, process). Why is it important to distinguish between them?

Answer: Types:

  1. Functional requirements:
  2. What the system should do
  3. Specific behaviors and functions

  4. Example: "System shall calculate tax"

  5. Quality requirements:

  6. How well the system should perform
  7. Performance, reliability, usability, security

  8. Example: "Response time shall be < 2 seconds"

  9. Platform requirements:

  10. Constraints on the environment
  11. Hardware, software, network

  12. Example: "System shall run on Windows 10"

  13. Process requirements:

  14. How the development should proceed
  15. Standards, methodologies, documentation
  16. Example: "Code shall follow Java coding standards"

Why distinguish: - Different stakeholders care about different types - Different validation methods - Different impact on architecture - Helps prioritize - Ensures complete coverage

Q11. What are the common problems in requirements gathering? How can they be addressed?

Answer: Common problems:

  1. Incomplete requirements:

  2. Solution: Use multiple techniques, involve all stakeholders

  3. Ambiguous requirements:

  4. Solution: Use precise language, examples, prototypes

  5. Conflicting requirements:

  6. Solution: Facilitate discussions, prioritize, find compromises

  7. Changing requirements:

  8. Solution: Expect change, use iterative approach, change control process

  9. Users don't know what they want:

  10. Solution: Prototyping, observation, iterative refinement

  11. Communication gaps:

  12. Solution: Domain analysis, common terminology, visual models

  13. Gold-plating:

  14. Solution: Focus on real problems, cost-benefit analysis

Q12. Explain the concept of scope creep. How can it be prevented or managed?

Answer: Scope creep is the uncontrolled expansion of project scope after the project has started.

Causes: - Poor initial requirements - Pressure from stakeholders - Lack of change control - "Just one more feature" mentality

Prevention/Management: 1. Clear initial scope: Well-defined requirements 2. Change control process: Formal process for evaluating changes 3. Prioritization: Focus on must-haves first 4. Stakeholder agreement: Everyone agrees on scope 5. Regular reviews: Monitor for scope changes 6. Impact analysis: Assess cost of each change 7. Communication: Keep stakeholders informed 8. Iterative delivery: Deliver in increments

docs.title: Short Answer Questions
docs.text:
Q1. What is an SRS document? What is its purpose?

Answer: An SRS (Software Requirements Specification) document is a formal document that describes what the software system will do.

Purpose: - Communicate requirements to all stakeholders - Basis for design and implementation - Foundation for testing - Reference for acceptance - Contract between customer and developer - Helps manage scope

Q2. List five characteristics of a good requirement (the "quality criteria" for requirements).

Answer: 1. Correct: Accurately describes needed functionality 2. Unambiguous: Only one interpretation 3. Complete: All necessary information included 4. Consistent: No conflicts with other requirements 5. Verifiable: Can be tested or inspected 6. Traceable: Can be traced to origin and implementation 7. Prioritized: Importance is indicated 8. Modifiable: Easy to change

Q3. What does it mean for a requirement to be verifiable? Give an example of a requirement that is NOT verifiable.

Answer: A requirement is verifiable if there is a finite, cost-effective way to check that it has been met.

Verifiable example: - "The system shall display search results within 3 seconds" - Can be tested by timing searches

NOT verifiable example: - "The system shall be user-friendly" - Too subjective; no clear way to verify

Better version: - "New users shall complete a task within 5 minutes with no more than 2 errors"

Q4. What is traceability in the context of requirements?

Answer: Traceability is the ability to track a requirement from its origin through implementation and testing.

Types: - Forward: Requirements → Design → Code → Tests - Backward: Tests → Code → Design → Requirements

Benefits: - Impact analysis for changes - Verification of completeness - Testing coverage - Maintenance support

Q5. What is a use case? How does it relate to requirements?

Answer: A use case describes a sequence of actions a system performs to yield an observable result of value to an actor.

Relationship to requirements: - Use cases capture functional requirements - Each use case represents a requirement or set of requirements - Use cases describe system behavior from user perspective - Help validate requirements with users - Provide basis for test cases

docs.title: Long Answer Questions
docs.text:
Q6. Describe the typical contents of an SRS document. What sections should it contain?

Answer: Typical SRS contents:

  1. Introduction
  2. Purpose
  3. Scope
  4. Definitions and acronyms

  5. References

  6. Overall Description

  7. Product perspective
  8. Product functions
  9. User characteristics
  10. Constraints

  11. Assumptions and dependencies

  12. Specific Requirements

  13. Functional requirements
  14. External interface requirements
  15. Performance requirements
  16. Design constraints
  17. Quality attributes

  18. Other requirements

  19. Appendices

  20. Supporting information
  21. Use cases
  22. Glossary

Q7. Explain the principles for writing good requirements documents as discussed in the textbook.

Answer: 1. Ensure benefit outweighs cost - Each requirement should add value 2. Contribute to problem solution - Must address a real need 3. Express clearly and consistently - Use clear language 4. Be unambiguous - Only one interpretation 5. Be consistent - No conflicts 6. Contribute to sufficient quality - Meet quality standards 7. Be developable with available resources - Feasible 8. Be verifiable - Can be tested 9. Be uniquely identifiable - Each has unique ID 10. Not over-constrain design - Allow design flexibility 11. Be sufficiently complete - Cover all needs 12. Organize effectively - Logical structure 13. Give clear rationale - Explain why 14. Obtain stakeholder agreement - Everyone agrees

Q8. What is the difference between user requirements and system requirements? How are they documented differently?

Answer:

User Requirements System Requirements Written for users/customers Written for developers High-level, in user language Detailed, technical Describe what users need Describe what system does Less formal More formal May use natural language May use formal notations

Documentation: - User requirements: In language users understand, focus on business value - System requirements: Precise, technical, may include models and specifications

Q9. Discuss the importance of requirements review. What should be checked during a requirements review?

Answer: Importance: - Catch errors early (cheaper to fix) - Ensure completeness - Get stakeholder agreement - Improve quality - Reduce risk

What to check: 1. Correctness - Does it match user needs? 2. Completeness - Is anything missing? 3. Consistency - Any conflicts? 4. Clarity - Is it understandable? 5. Verifiability - Can it be tested? 6. Traceability - Can it be traced? 7. Feasibility - Can it be implemented? 8. Priority - Is importance indicated? 9. Ambiguity - Any unclear statements? 10. Redundancy - Any duplication?

Q10. Explain how requirements should be organized in an SRS document for maximum clarity and usability.

Answer: Organization principles:

  1. Logical grouping:
  2. Group by feature
  3. Group by user type

  4. Group by subsystem

  5. Hierarchical structure:

  6. High-level requirements first

  7. Detailed requirements follow

  8. Unique identification:

  9. Each requirement has unique ID

  10. Enables traceability

  11. Consistent format:

  12. Same template for all requirements

  13. Includes ID, description, priority, rationale

  14. Cross-references:

  15. Link related requirements

  16. Link to use cases

  17. Index and glossary:

  18. Easy to find requirements
  19. Common terms defined

docs.title: Short Answer Questions
docs.text:
Q1. What is requirement modeling? Why is it important?

Answer: Requirement modeling is the creation of abstract representations (models) of the system to understand and communicate requirements.

Importance: - Visual communication - Abstraction from details - Identify gaps and inconsistencies - Basis for design - Validate understanding - Common understanding among stakeholders

Q2. List three types of models that can be used for requirement modeling.

Answer: 1. Use case models - Show system functionality from user perspective 2. Domain models (class diagrams) - Show concepts and relationships 3. Activity diagrams - Show business processes 4. State diagrams - Show object lifecycle 5. Sequence diagrams - Show interactions

Q3. What is the purpose of a domain model?

Answer: A domain model shows: - Key concepts (classes) in the problem domain - Relationships between concepts - Attributes of concepts

Purpose: - Understand the domain - Common vocabulary - Foundation for design - Communication with domain experts - Identify key abstractions

Q4. What is the difference between analysis and design in the context of modeling?

Answer:

Analysis Design Focus on WHAT Focus on HOW Understand requirements Plan implementation Domain-oriented Solution-oriented Technology-independent Technology-specific "What should the system do?" "How will the system do it?"

Q5. What is OCL (Object Constraint Language)? What is it used for?

Answer: OCL is a formal language for expressing constraints and queries on UML models.

Used for: - Specifying invariants (conditions that must always be true) - Pre and post conditions - Guard conditions - Derivation rules - Query expressions

Example:

context Employee inv:
  self.age >= 18

docs.title: Long Answer Questions
docs.text:
Q6. Describe how UML can be used for requirement modeling. What diagrams are most useful at this stage?

Answer: UML for requirement modeling:

  1. Use case diagrams:
  2. Capture functional requirements
  3. Show system scope

  4. Identify actors

  5. Activity diagrams:

  6. Model business processes
  7. Show workflow

  8. Identify system boundaries

  9. Domain class diagrams:

  10. Identify key concepts
  11. Show relationships

  12. Build common vocabulary

  13. State diagrams:

  14. Model lifecycle of key objects

  15. Identify events and transitions

  16. Sequence diagrams:

  17. Show interactions for key scenarios
  18. Validate use cases

Q7. Explain the process of creating a domain model. What elements should be included?

Answer: Process: 1. Identify key concepts (nouns from requirements) 2. Identify attributes 3. Identify relationships 4. Determine multiplicities 5. Refine and validate

Elements to include: - Classes: Key concepts (e.g., Customer, Order, Product) - Attributes: Properties of classes - Associations: Relationships between classes - Multiplicities: How many instances participate - Association classes: When relationship has attributes - Generalizations: "Is-a" relationships

Q8. Discuss the relationship between requirements and models. How do models help in understanding and communicating requirements?

Answer: Relationship: - Models are visual representations of requirements - Multiple models may represent same requirements - Models provide different perspectives

How models help:

  1. Understanding:
  2. Abstraction removes details
  3. Visual representation easier to understand

  4. Different perspectives reveal different aspects

  5. Communication:

  6. Common visual language
  7. Bridge between technical and non-technical stakeholders

  8. Reduce ambiguity

  9. Validation:

  10. Stakeholders can review models
  11. Identify missing or incorrect requirements

  12. Early feedback

  13. Foundation for design:

  14. Models evolve into design
  15. Maintain traceability

docs.text:
Q1. What is a use case diagram? What does it show?

Answer: A use case diagram is a UML behavioral diagram that shows: - System functionality (use cases) - Users/External systems (actors) that interact with the system - Relationships between use cases and actors

It shows WHAT the system does from an external perspective.

Q2. Draw the UML notation for various use case diagram elements.

Answer:

Actor:         Use Case:         <<include>>:
  |              ______              ______
 /|\            /      \            /      \
  |    -------->( Use    )    ----->( Included)
 / \            \ Case /            \______/
 Stick figure    \______/
                Oval

<<extend>>:      System Boundary:
  ______         +------------------+
 /      \       |                  |
( Extending)--->|  Use Case        |
 \______/       |                  |
                +------------------+
                Rectangle

Q3. What is the difference between <\> and <\> relationships? Give an example of each.

Answer:

<\> <> Base use case always includes the included use case Extension use case adds behavior conditionally Mandatory Optional Arrow points to included use case Arrow points from extending to base

<\> example: - "Place Order" includes "Verify Credit Card" - Verification always happens

<\> example: - "Search Product" is extended by "Show Recommendations" - Recommendations shown only sometimes

Q4. What is a generalized actor? How is it represented?

Answer: A generalized actor is an actor that inherits from another actor.

Representation: - Hollow triangle arrow pointing to parent actor - Child actor inherits parent's associations

Example:

      User
        ^
       /|
      / |
  Customer  Administrator

Both Customer and Administrator can do what User can do.

Q5. What is a system boundary in a use case diagram?

Answer: A system boundary is a rectangle that: - Encloses the use cases - Separates the system from external actors - Shows scope of the system - Named with the system name

Q6. What are the guidelines for naming use cases?

Answer: 1. Use verb-noun format (e.g., "Place Order", "Withdraw Cash") 2. Name from actor's perspective 3. Use active voice 4. Be specific and descriptive 5. Avoid technical jargon 6. Keep it concise 7. Use consistent terminology

docs.title: Long Answer Questions
docs.text:
Q7. Describe the components of a use case diagram. Explain each component with examples.

Answer: Components:

  1. Actors:
  2. External entities that interact with system
  3. Can be people, other systems, devices

  4. Example: Customer, Bank System

  5. Use Cases:

  6. System functionality
  7. Oval shape

  8. Example: "Place Order", "Check Balance"

  9. System Boundary:

  10. Rectangle enclosing use cases

  11. Shows system scope

  12. Associations:

  13. Lines connecting actors to use cases

  14. Show participation

  15. <\> relationship:

  16. One use case always includes another

  17. Arrow to included use case

  18. <\> relationship:

  19. One use case optionally extends another

  20. Arrow from extending to base

  21. Generalization:

  22. Actor or use case inheritance

    23. Q8. Explain how to identify actors for a system. What questions should you ask?

    Answer: Questions to identify actors:

    1. Who uses the system?
    2. Who installs the system?
    3. Who starts and shuts down the system?
    4. Who maintains the system?
    5. What other systems interact with this system?
    6. Who gets information from the system?
    7. Who provides information to the system?
    8. What happens at specific times?

    Types of actors: - Primary actors: Initiate use cases - Secondary actors: Participate but don't initiate - External systems: Other software systems

    Q9. What is the relationship between use cases and requirements? How do use cases help in requirements gathering?

    Answer: Relationship: - Use cases capture functional requirements - Each use case represents one or more requirements - Use cases organize requirements by user goal

    How use cases help:

    1. User-centric:
    2. Focus on what users want to achieve

    3. Easy for users to understand and validate

    4. Complete picture:

    5. Show all ways users interact with system

    6. Help identify missing requirements

    7. Communication:

    8. Common language between users and developers

    9. Visual representation

    10. Test basis:

    11. Use cases become test cases

    12. Ensure all functionality is tested

    13. Scope management:

    14. Clear boundaries
    15. Easy to identify gold-plating

    Q10-Q12. Draw a use case diagram for various scenarios.

    Answer:

    Library Management System:

|       |                   |             |
|       |    [Check Fines]  |             |
|       +---------><--------+             |
|                                         |
|  [Search Catalog]   [Renew Book]        |
+-----------------------------------------+
       ^                ^
       |                |
    Member         Librarian

docs.title: Short Answer Questions
docs.text:
Q1. What is a sequence diagram? What does it show?

Answer: A sequence diagram is a UML interaction diagram that shows: - Objects participating in an interaction - Messages exchanged between objects - Order of messages over time

It shows HOW objects collaborate to achieve a goal.

Q2. Draw and label the main elements of a sequence diagram.

Answer:

Object1:    Object2:    Object3:
  |           |           |
  |           |           |
  |---------->|           |  message1()
  |           |           |
  |           |---------->|  message2()
  |           |           |
  |<----------|           |  return
  |           |           |
  |           |<----------|  return
  |           |           |
  |           |           X  destruction

Lifeline: Vertical dotted line
Activation box: Rectangle on lifeline
Message: Horizontal arrow

Q3. What is a lifeline in a sequence diagram?

Answer: A lifeline is: - A vertical dotted line representing an object's existence over time - Shows when an object is created and destroyed - Messages are drawn between lifelines - Time progresses downward

Q4. What is an activation box? What does it represent?

Answer: An activation box is: - A narrow rectangle on a lifeline - Shows when an object is active (executing) - Represents a method call being executed - Can be nested to show nested calls

Q5. What is the difference between a synchronous and asynchronous message? How are they represented differently?

Answer:

Synchronous Asynchronous Sender waits for response Sender continues immediately Blocking call Non-blocking Solid arrow with filled head Open arrow head Return message shown No return message

Example:

Synchronous:    Asynchronous:
  ----->>         ----->
  <-----

Q6. What is a combined fragment? List three types of interaction operators.

Answer: A combined fragment groups sets of messages together to show control structures.

Interaction operators: 1. alt - Alternative (if-then-else) 2. opt - Optional (if-then) 3. loop - Iteration 4. par - Parallel 5. break - Break loop 6. seq - Weak sequencing 7. strict - Strict sequencing

Q7. What is object destruction? How is it shown in a sequence diagram?

Answer: Object destruction shows when an object is deleted.

Representation: - Large X at bottom of lifeline - Can be triggered by a destroy message - Lifeline ends at destruction

docs.title: Long Answer Questions
docs.text:
Q8. Describe the components of a sequence diagram. Explain how to read and create one.

Answer: Components:

  1. Objects/Participants:
  2. Shown at top

  3. Format: "name:Class"

  4. Lifelines:

  5. Vertical dotted lines

  6. Show object existence

  7. Activation boxes:

  8. Show method execution

  9. Nested for nested calls

  10. Messages:

  11. Horizontal arrows

  12. Labeled with method name

  13. Return messages:

  14. Dashed arrows

  15. Show return values

  16. Combined fragments:

  17. Control structures

How to read: - Start at top - Follow messages down - Time flows downward

How to create: 1. Identify objects involved 2. Determine message sequence 3. Draw lifelines 4. Add messages 5. Add activations 6. Add control structures if needed

Q9. Explain the different types of messages that can appear in a sequence diagram.

Answer:

  1. Synchronous message:
  2. Blocking call
  3. Sender waits

  4. Solid arrow with filled head

  5. Asynchronous message:

  6. Non-blocking
  7. Sender continues

  8. Open arrow head

  9. Return message:

  10. Response to synchronous call
  11. Dashed arrow

  12. Often omitted (implied)

  13. Create message:

  14. Creates new object

  15. Arrow to new object's lifeline

  16. Destroy message:

  17. Destroys object

  18. Arrow to X on lifeline

  19. Reply message:

  20. Explicit return
  21. Dashed arrow

Q10. What are combined fragments? Describe at least four types of interaction operators and when to use each.

Answer:

  1. alt (alternative):
  2. If-then-else logic
  3. Multiple guarded alternatives

  4. Use when: Different behavior based on condition

  5. opt (option):

  6. Optional behavior
  7. Single guarded region

  8. Use when: Behavior may or may not occur

  9. loop:

  10. Repeated behavior
  11. Has guard condition

  12. Use when: Iteration needed

  13. par (parallel):

  14. Concurrent behavior
  15. Multiple regions execute simultaneously

  16. Use when: Parallel processing

  17. break:

  18. Exit enclosing loop

  19. Use when: Early exit condition

  20. seq (weak sequencing):

  21. Default sequencing
  22. Use when: Standard message ordering

Q11. Draw a sequence diagram for various scenarios.

Answer:

   |         |         |           |

   |         |-validatePIN()---->|
   |         |         |         |

   |         |         |           |

Q12. Explain the difference between a sequence diagram and a communication diagram. When would you use each?

Answer:

Sequence Diagram Communication Diagram Emphasizes time ordering Emphasizes relationships Vertical time axis No time axis Better for complex scenarios Better for showing structure Shows object lifelines Shows object links Easier to read for timing More compact

When to use: - Sequence: When timing and order are important - Communication: When showing object relationships is important

docs.title: Short Answer Questions
docs.text:
Q1. What is a state diagram? What does it show?

Answer: A state diagram is a UML behavioral diagram that shows: - States an object can be in - Events that cause state changes - Transitions between states - Actions on transitions or in states

It shows the lifecycle of an object.

Q2. Draw and label the main elements of a state diagram.

Answer:

                    event[guard]/action
    +--------+ ------------------------> +--------+
    | State1 |                            | State2 |
    | entry/ |                            | do/    |
    |  init  |                            |activity|
    | exit/  | <------------------------- |        |
    |cleanup |      anotherEvent           +--------+
    +--------+
         |
         | initial
         v
    *-----
   Start state

State: Rounded rectangle
Transition: Arrow with label
Start state: Filled circle
End state: Circle with dot

Q3. What is the difference between a state and an activity?

Answer: | State | Activity | |-------|----------| | A condition or situation | Something that happens in a state | | "Being in a state" | "Doing something" | | Represents a mode | Represents ongoing work | | Example: "Idle" | Example: "Monitoring sensors" |

In UML, activities are shown with "do/" prefix in a state.

Q4. What is a transition? What are its components?

Answer: A transition is a change from one state to another.

Components: 1. Source state: State leaving 2. Target state: State entering 3. Event: Trigger for transition (optional) 4. Guard condition: Boolean condition (optional) 5. Action: Activity performed during transition (optional)

Syntax: event[guard]/action

Q5. What is a guard condition? How is it represented?

Answer: A guard condition is a boolean expression that must be true for the transition to occur.

Representation: - In square brackets - Part of transition label

Example: withdraw[balance >= amount]

Q6. What is a self-transition? Give an example.

Answer: A self-transition is a transition from a state back to itself.

Example:

+---------+
|  Idle   |<---/refreshDisplay
+---------+

In an ATM, while in "Waiting for PIN" state, a timeout event might trigger a "display reminder" action but stay in the same state.

Q7. What are entry and exit actions? How are they specified?

Answer: Entry actions: Performed when entering a state Exit actions: Performed when leaving a state

Specification: - Entry: entry/actionName - Exit: exit/actionName

Example:

+-----------------+
|   Connected     |
| entry/startTimer|
| exit/stopTimer  |
+-----------------+

Q8. What is a composite state (superstate)? What are its advantages?

Answer: A composite state is a state that contains substates.

Advantages: 1. Reduces complexity by nesting 2. Shows hierarchical structure 3. Can have transitions to/from superstate 4. Substates inherit transitions from superstate 5. Better organization of complex behavior

docs.text:
Q9. Describe the components of a state diagram. Explain each element with examples.

Answer: Components:

  1. States:

  5. Transitions:

  12. End state:

  15. Activities:

  16. entry/ - action on entry
  17. exit/ - action on exit

  18. do/ - ongoing activity

  19. Events:

  20. Triggers for transitions

  21. External or internal

  22. Guard conditions:

  23. Boolean conditions
  24. Control whether transition occurs

Q10. Explain the difference between Moore and Mealy machines. Which one does UML state diagrams follow?

Answer:

Moore Machine Mealy Machine Output depends only on state Output depends on state and input Actions in states Actions on transitions

UML state diagrams: - Follow both approaches - Can have actions in states (Moore) - Can have actions on transitions (Mealy) - Most flexible approach

Q12. What is the difference between a state diagram and an activity diagram? When would you use each?

State Diagram Activity Diagram Shows object lifecycle Shows workflow/process Focus on states Focus on activities Event-driven Activity-driven For single object For multiple objects/roles Reactive systems Business processes

When to use: - State diagram: Modeling object behavior, reactive systems - Activity diagram: Modeling business processes, workflows

docs.title: Short Answer Questions
docs.text:
Q1. What is an activity diagram? What does it show?

Answer: An activity diagram is a UML behavioral diagram that shows: - Workflow or business process - Sequence of activities - Parallel and conditional flows - Decision points

It shows the flow of control and data through a system.

Q2. Draw and label the main elements of an activity diagram.

Answer:

*--->[Activity]---><>--->[Activity2]
Start  Action      Decision

[Activity3]---><>--->[Activity4]
             Fork (parallel)

[Activity5]--->*
             Join
              End

Swimlanes:
+---------+---------+
|  User   | System  |
+---------+---------+
|[Action] |         |
|         |[Action] |
+---------+---------+

Q3. What is the difference between an action and an activity?

Answer:

Action Activity Single step Can contain multiple actions Atomic Can be decomposed Simple Complex No internal structure Has internal structure

In UML, both are shown as rounded rectangles, but activities can be expanded.

Q4. What is a fork node? What is a join node?

Answer: Fork node: - Splits one flow into multiple parallel flows - All outgoing flows execute concurrently - Single input, multiple outputs

Join node: - Combines multiple parallel flows into one - Waits for all incoming flows to complete - Multiple inputs, single output

Q5. What is a decision node? How is it different from a merge node?

Answer: Decision node: - Splits flow based on guard conditions - One input, multiple outputs - Only one output path taken

Merge node: - Combines multiple alternative flows - Multiple inputs, one output - No synchronization

Difference: - Decision splits, Merge combines - Decision has guards, Merge doesn't

Q6. What are swimlanes? What is their purpose?

Answer: Swimlanes are vertical or horizontal partitions that show: - Which object or role performs each activity - Responsibility assignment - Parallel processing by different entities

Purpose: - Show who does what - Organize complex diagrams - Show handoffs between roles - Improve readability

Q7. What is signal sending and signal receipt? How are they represented?

Answer: Signal sending: - Sends signal to external entity - Convex pentagon - Labeled with signal name

Signal receipt: - Waits for signal from external entity - Concave pentagon - Labeled with signal name
