docs.title: Short Answer Questions
docs.text:
Q1. What is UML? What is its purpose?

Answer: UML (Unified Modeling Language) is a standardized visual modeling language for software systems.

Purpose: - Communicate system design - Visualize system structure and behavior - Specify system details - Document systems - Standard notation for software engineering

Q2. List the 13 types of UML diagrams and categorize them as structural or behavioral.

Answer: Structural (6): 1. Class diagram 2. Object diagram 3. Component diagram 4. Deployment diagram 5. Package diagram 6. Composite structure diagram

Behavioral (7): 1. Use case diagram 2. Activity diagram 3. State diagram 4. Sequence diagram 5. Communication diagram 6. Interaction overview diagram 7. Timing diagram

Q3. What is the difference between a structural diagram and a behavioral diagram?

Answer:

Structural Diagram Behavioral Diagram Shows static structure Shows dynamic behavior What exists What happens Classes, components, relationships Interactions, activities, states Snapshot in time Over time

Q4. What is the purpose of a package diagram?

Answer: A package diagram shows: - Organization of model elements into packages - Dependencies between packages - High-level system structure

Purpose: - Organize large systems - Show module structure - Manage complexity - Show layering

Q5. What is a deployment diagram? What does it show?

Answer: A deployment diagram shows: - Physical architecture of the system - Hardware nodes - Software components deployed on nodes - Communication between nodes

Shows: - Servers, clients, devices - Software installation - Network topology - Communication protocols

Q6. What is a component diagram?

Answer: A component diagram shows: - System components (modules, libraries) - Interfaces provided and required - Dependencies between components

Purpose: - Show system decomposition - Interface definition - Reusable components - Implementation structure

docs.title: Long Answer Questions
docs.text:
Q7. Describe the different types of UML diagrams. For each, explain its purpose and when it should be used.

Answer:

Structural Diagrams:

  1. Class diagram:
  2. Shows classes and relationships

  3. Use for: System structure, database design

  4. Object diagram:

  5. Shows object instances

  6. Use for: Examples, testing scenarios

  7. Component diagram:

  8. Shows system components

  9. Use for: Implementation structure

  10. Deployment diagram:

  11. Shows hardware and deployment

  12. Use for: System architecture

  13. Package diagram:

  14. Shows package organization
  15. Use for: Large system organization

Behavioral Diagrams:

  1. Use case diagram:
  2. Shows system functionality

  3. Use for: Requirements, scope

  4. Activity diagram:

  5. Shows workflows

  6. Use for: Business processes

  7. State diagram:

  8. Shows object states

  9. Use for: Reactive objects

  10. Sequence diagram:

  11. Shows object interactions

  12. Use for: Detailed scenarios

  13. Communication diagram:

    • Shows object collaborations
    • Use for: Emphasizing relationships

Q8. Explain how the different UML diagrams work together to provide a complete model of a system.

Answer: UML diagrams provide multiple perspectives:

  1. Requirements perspective:
  2. Use case diagrams capture requirements

  3. Activity diagrams show processes

  4. Structural perspective:

  5. Class diagrams show static structure

  6. Package diagrams show organization

  7. Behavioral perspective:

  8. Sequence diagrams show interactions

  9. State diagrams show object lifecycles

  10. Implementation perspective:

  11. Component diagrams show modules
  12. Deployment diagrams show hardware

Working together: - Use cases drive class design - Classes participate in sequences - States define object behavior - Components implement classes - Deployment hosts components

Q9. Discuss the importance of visual modeling in software engineering. What are the benefits of using UML?

Answer: Importance of visual modeling: - Software is abstract - models make it tangible - Communication tool - Abstraction from code - Early validation - Documentation

Benefits of UML: 1. Standard notation: Everyone understands 2. Multiple perspectives: Different views of system 3. Tool support: Many CASE tools available 4. Communication: Between stakeholders 5. Abstraction: Think at higher level 6. Documentation: Living documentation 7. Code generation: Some tools generate code 8. Reverse engineering: Generate models from code

Continue to Part 4 for Relationships and Design Patterns

docs.title: Short Answer Questions
docs.text:
Q1. What is an association in UML? How is it represented?

Answer: An association is a relationship between classes showing that objects of one class are connected to objects of another.

Representation: - Solid line between classes - Can have name - Can have direction arrow - Can have multiplicity

Q2. What is multiplicity? List the common multiplicity values and their meanings.

Answer: Multiplicity specifies how many instances of one class can be associated with instances of another.

Common values:

Notation Meaning 1 Exactly one 0..1 Zero or one * Zero or more 1..* One or more n Exactly n n..m Between n and m

Q3. What is the difference between unidirectional and bidirectional associations?

Answer:

Unidirectional Bidirectional Only one class knows about the other Both classes know about each other Arrow points to known class No arrow Lower coupling Higher coupling Example: Person -> Car Example: Person -- Car

Q4. What is an association class? When is it needed?

Answer: An association class is a class that is also an association.

Needed when: - The association itself has attributes - The association has operations - The association has its own identity

Example: - Employee works for Company - The "works for" association has attributes: salary, startDate

Q5. What is aggregation? How is it different from a regular association?

Answer: Aggregation is a "whole-part" relationship where the part can exist independently of the whole.

Difference from association:

Association Aggregation "knows a" "has a" No ownership Weak ownership Parts independent Parts can exist alone Hollow diamond Hollow diamond on whole side

Example: - University has Departments - If University closes, Departments may still exist

Q6. What is composition? How is it different from aggregation?

Answer: Composition is a strong "whole-part" relationship where the part cannot exist without the whole.

Difference from aggregation:

Aggregation Composition Weak ownership Strong ownership Parts can exist alone Parts cannot exist alone Hollow diamond Filled diamond "has a" "contains a"

Example: - House has Rooms - If House destroyed, Rooms are destroyed too

Q7. What is generalization? How is it represented in UML?

Answer: Generalization is an "is-a" relationship where a subclass inherits from a superclass.

Representation: - Hollow triangle arrow pointing to superclass - Subclass at arrow tail

Example:

      Vehicle
        ^
       /|
      / |
    Car  Truck

Q8. What is the difference between generalization and inheritance?

Answer:

Generalization Inheritance UML concept Programming concept Relationship between classes Mechanism to reuse code "Is-a" relationship Implementation technique Modeling concept Language feature

Generalization is the model; inheritance is the implementation.

Q9. What is a dependency relationship? When is it used?

Answer: A dependency is a weaker relationship where one class uses another.

Used when: - One class temporarily uses another - Parameter type - Local variable - Return type

Representation: - Dashed arrow

Example:

Controller - - - > Service

Q10. What is a realization relationship? Give an example.

Answer: Realization is a relationship between a specification (interface) and its implementation.

Example:

      <<interface>>
      PaymentProcessor
            ^
            |
       +----+----+
   PayPal    CreditCard

PayPal and CreditCard realize (implement) PaymentProcessor interface.

docs.title: Long Answer Questions
docs.text:
Q11. Compare and contrast association, aggregation, and composition. Give examples of each and explain when to use them.

Answer:

Aspect Association Aggregation Composition Relationship "knows a" "has a" "contains a" Strength Weak Medium Strong Ownership None Weak Strong Lifetime Independent Part can exist alone Part dies with whole UML Line Hollow diamond Filled diamond

Examples:

Association:

Professor --- teaches --- Course

Professor knows about Course, no ownership.

Aggregation:

University <>--- Department

University has Departments, but Departments can exist independently.

Composition:

House <*>--- Room

House contains Rooms; Rooms cannot exist without House.

When to use: - Association: Simple relationship, no ownership - Aggregation: Whole-part, parts reusable - Composition: Whole-part, parts not reusable

Q12. Explain the concept of multiplicity in detail. How do you determine the appropriate multiplicity for a relationship?

Answer: Multiplicity defines how many instances participate in a relationship.

Determining multiplicity:

  1. Analyze business rules:
  2. "A customer can have multiple orders" -> 1..*

  3. "An order belongs to exactly one customer" -> 1

  4. Consider real-world constraints:

  5. Physical limitations

  6. Business policies

  7. Ask questions:

  8. Can there be zero?
  9. Is there a maximum?

  10. Is there a minimum?

  11. Examples:

  12. Person -- Address: 1..* (person has at least one address)
  13. Order -- OrderLine: 1..* (order has at least one line)
  14. Employee -- Manager: 0..1 (employee may or may not have manager)

Q13. Describe the different types of relationships that can exist between classes in UML. For each, explain its semantics and notation.

Answer:

  1. Association:
  2. Semantics: "knows a"

  3. Notation: Solid line

  4. Directed Association:

  5. Semantics: One-way knowledge

  6. Notation: Solid line with arrow

  7. Aggregation:

  8. Semantics: "has a" (weak)

  9. Notation: Hollow diamond on whole

  10. Composition:

  11. Semantics: "contains a" (strong)

  12. Notation: Filled diamond on whole

  13. Generalization:

  14. Semantics: "is a"

  15. Notation: Hollow triangle arrow

  16. Dependency:

  17. Semantics: "uses"

  18. Notation: Dashed arrow

  19. Realization:

  20. Semantics: "implements"
  21. Notation: Dashed arrow with hollow triangle

Q14. Explain the concept of navigability in associations. What are the implications of navigability for implementation?

Answer: Navigability indicates whether one class can access another through the association.

Representation: - Arrow shows direction of navigation - No arrow = bidirectional

Implications for implementation:

Navigability Implementation Unidirectional Reference in one class only Bidirectional References in both classes

Example:

Order -----> OrderLine
  • Order has reference to OrderLine
  • OrderLine doesn't know about Order
  • Lower coupling

Q15. Draw a class diagram showing various relationships.

Answer:

|       |                            |    |          |      |

docs.title: General Design Patterns
docs.text:
Q1. What is a design pattern? What are the three main categories of design patterns?

Answer: A design pattern is a reusable solution to a commonly occurring problem in software design.

Three categories (GoF): 1. Creational: Object creation mechanisms 2. Structural: Class and object composition 3. Behavioral: Communication between objects

Q2. What are the benefits of using design patterns?

Answer: 1. Proven solutions: Tested and validated 2. Reusability: Apply same solution to similar problems 3. Communication: Common vocabulary 4. Maintainability: Well-structured code 5. Reduced complexity: Elegant solutions 6. Best practices: Follow good design principles

Q3. What is the difference between a design pattern and a framework?

Answer:

Design Pattern Framework Abstract solution Concrete implementation Language-independent Language-specific Reusable idea Reusable code Smaller scope Larger scope Example: Singleton Example: Spring Framework

docs.title: Facade Pattern
docs.text:
Q4. What is the Facade pattern? What problem does it solve?

Answer: The Facade pattern provides a simplified interface to a complex subsystem.

Problem it solves: - Complex subsystem with many classes - Client code becomes complex when using subsystem directly - Tight coupling between client and subsystem

Solution: - Single entry point (facade) - Simplified interface - Reduced coupling

Q5. What is the intent of the Facade pattern?

Answer: Intent (GoF): "Provide a unified interface to a set of interfaces in a subsystem. Facade defines a higher-level interface that makes the subsystem easier to use."

Q6. Give an example scenario where the Facade pattern would be useful.

Answer: Scenario: A home theater system with multiple components: - Amplifier - DVD Player - Projector - Screen - Lights

Without Facade: Client must interact with each component separately.

With Facade:

HomeTheaterFacade theater = new HomeTheaterFacade(amp, dvd, projector, screen, lights);
theater.watchMovie("Inception"); // Simplified!

Q7. How does the Facade pattern reduce coupling?

Answer: - Client depends only on Facade, not on subsystem classes - Subsystem can change without affecting client - Facade encapsulates subsystem complexity - Single point of contact

docs.title: Observer Pattern
docs.text:
Q8. What is the Observer pattern? What problem does it solve?

Answer: The Observer pattern defines a one-to-many dependency between objects.

Problem it solves: - One object (subject) changes state - Multiple objects (observers) need to be notified - Tight coupling if subject knows all observers directly

Solution: - Subject maintains list of observers - Observers register themselves - Subject notifies all observers when state changes

Q9. What are the main components of the Observer pattern?

Answer: 1. Subject: - Knows its observers - Provides interface for attaching/detaching observers

  1. Observer:

  2. Interface for objects that should be notified

  3. ConcreteSubject:

  4. Stores state

  5. Sends notification when state changes

  6. ConcreteObserver:

  7. Maintains reference to ConcreteSubject
  8. Implements update interface

Q10. Give a real-world example of the Observer pattern.

Answer: Newsletter subscription: - Publisher (Subject) sends newsletters - Subscribers (Observers) receive newsletters - Subscribers can subscribe/unsubscribe - When new newsletter published, all subscribers notified

Stock price monitoring: - Stock (Subject) price changes - Multiple displays (Observers) show updated price - New displays can be added without changing Stock class

Q11. How does the Observer pattern reduce coupling?

Answer: - Subject doesn't know concrete observers - Only knows Observer interface - Observers can be added/removed dynamically - Subject and observers can vary independently - Supports open/closed principle

Q12. What is the difference between push and pull models in the Observer pattern?

Answer:

Push Model Pull Model Subject sends data to observers Observers request data from subject update(data) update() Observers receive all data Observers get only what they need Less flexible More flexible Simpler for observers More efficient

docs.title: Adapter Pattern
docs.text:
Q13. What is the Adapter pattern? What problem does it solve?

Answer: The Adapter pattern converts the interface of a class into another interface that clients expect.

Problem it solves: - Incompatible interfaces - Want to use existing class but interface doesn't match - Can't modify existing class (legacy, third-party)

Solution: - Create adapter that wraps existing class - Adapter implements target interface - Client uses adapter, adapter delegates to adaptee

Q14. What are the two types of Adapter pattern? Explain each.

Answer:

  1. Object Adapter:
  2. Uses composition
  3. Adapter holds reference to adaptee

  4. More flexible (can adapt subclasses)

  5. Class Adapter:

  6. Uses inheritance
  7. Adapter inherits from adaptee
  8. Less flexible (requires multiple inheritance in some languages)

Q15. Give an example scenario where the Adapter pattern would be useful.

Answer: Scenario: Integrating a legacy payment system with new e-commerce application.

Legacy system:

class LegacyPayment {
    void makePayment(double amount) { ... }
}

New system expects:

interface PaymentProcessor {
    void processPayment(BigDecimal amount);
}

Adapter:

class PaymentAdapter implements PaymentProcessor {
    private LegacyPayment legacy;

    void processPayment(BigDecimal amount) {
        legacy.makePayment(amount.doubleValue());
    }
}

Q16. How does the Adapter pattern improve reuse and flexibility?

Answer: - Allows reuse of existing classes with incompatible interfaces - No need to modify existing code - Can adapt multiple classes to same interface - Client code uses standard interface - Easy to swap implementations - Supports open/closed principle

docs.title: Long Answer Questions
docs.text:
Q17. Describe the Facade pattern in detail.

Answer: Intent: Provide a unified interface to a set of interfaces in a subsystem.

When to use: - Simplify complex subsystem - Layer system - Decouple subsystems

Structure:

+----------+
|  Client  |
+-----+----+
      | uses
      v
+----------+
|  Facade  |<-----------+
+-----+----+            |
      | knows           |
      v                 |
+----------+  +----------+  +----------+
|SubsystemA|  |SubsystemB|  |SubsystemC|
+----------+  +----------+  +----------+

Participants: - Facade: Knows subsystem responsibilities, delegates requests - Subsystem classes: Implement functionality, handle work

Benefits: - Shields clients from subsystem complexity - Promotes weak coupling - Doesn't prevent direct subsystem access

Drawbacks: - Facade can become a "god object" - May limit flexibility if overused

Q18. Describe the Observer pattern in detail.

Answer: Intent: Define a one-to-many dependency between objects so that when one object changes state, all its dependents are notified and updated automatically.

When to use: - One object changes, others need to know - Don't know how many objects need to change - Objects should be loosely coupled

Structure:

+-----------------+         +-------------+
|  <<interface>>  |         |  <<interface|
|    Subject      |<--------|   Observer  |
+-----------------+         +-------------+
| attach(Observer)|         |   update()  |
|detach(Observer) |         +------+------+
|    notify()     |                |
+--------+--------+                |
         | implements               | implements
         v                          v
+-----------------+         +-------------+
| ConcreteSubject |         |ConcreteObserver
+-----------------+         +-------------+
|   getState()    |-------->|   update()  |
|   setState()    |         |             |
+-----------------+         +-------------+

Participants: - Subject: Knows observers, provides attach/detach interface - Observer: Interface for notification - ConcreteSubject: Stores state, notifies observers - ConcreteObserver: Maintains reference, implements update

Benefits: - Abstract coupling between Subject and Observer - Support for broadcast communication - Observers can be added/removed dynamically

Drawbacks: - Unexpected updates - Memory leaks if observers not detached - Update order dependencies

Q19. Describe the Adapter pattern in detail.

Answer: Intent: Convert the interface of a class into another interface clients expect. Adapter lets classes work together that couldn't otherwise because of incompatible interfaces.

When to use: - Use existing class with incompatible interface - Create reusable class that cooperates with unforeseen classes - Use several existing subclasses, but adapting their interface is impractical

Structure (Object Adapter):

+----------+
|  Client  |
+-----+----+
      | uses
      v
+----------+
|  Target  |<-----------+
| interface|            |
+-----+----+            |
      | implements      |
      v                 |
+----------+            |
|  Adapter |------------+
+----------+
      | uses
      v
+----------+
|  Adaptee |
|specific  |
|Request() |
+----------+

Participants: - Target: Interface client expects - Adapter: Adapts Adaptee to Target interface - Adaptee: Existing interface to be adapted - Client: Uses Target interface

Benefits: - Reuse existing classes - Add flexibility - No modification to adaptee

Drawbacks: - Additional complexity - May need multiple adapters

Q20. Compare and contrast the Facade, Observer, and Adapter patterns.

Answer:

Aspect Facade Observer Adapter Category Structural Behavioral Structural Purpose Simplify interface Notify changes Convert interface Problem Complex subsystem State change notification Incompatible interfaces Solution Unified interface Subscription mechanism Interface translation Coupling Reduces Reduces Reduces Flexibility Hides complexity Dynamic registration Enables reuse

When to use: - Facade: Complex subsystem needs simple interface - Observer: One-to-many notification needed - Adapter: Need to use class with incompatible interface

Q21. Explain how design patterns promote good software design principles such as low coupling and high cohesion.

Answer:

Low Coupling: - Facade: Client depends only on Facade, not subsystem - Observer: Subject only knows Observer interface - Adapter: Client depends on Target, not Adaptee

High Cohesion: - Facade: Each subsystem class has single responsibility - Observer: Subject manages state, Observer handles notification - Adapter: Adapter only handles interface translation

Other principles: - Open/Closed: Add new observers/adapters without changing existing code - Single Responsibility: Each pattern component has one job - Dependency Inversion: Depend on abstractions

Q22. Draw a class diagram showing the structure of the three patterns.

Answer:

Facade Pattern:

+----------+
|  Client  |--------------+
+----------+              |
                          |
                    +-----+------+
                    |   Facade   |
                    +------------+
                    | operation()|
                    +-----+------+
                          |
        +-----------------+-----------------+
        |                 |                 |
   +----+----+      +-----+-----+     +----+----+
   |Subsystem|      |Subsystem2 |     |Subsystem|
   |   A     |      |     B     |     |    C    |
   +---------+      +-----------+     +---------+

Observer Pattern:

+-----------------+         +-------------+
|    Subject      |<--------|   Observer  |
+-----------------+         +-------------+
| attach(Observer)|         |   update()  |
|detach(Observer) |         +------+------+
|    notify()     |                |
+--------+--------+                |
         |                         |
         v                         v
+-----------------+         +-------------+
| ConcreteSubject |         |ConcreteObserver
+-----------------+         +-------------+
|   getState()    |         |   update()  |
|   setState()    |         |             |
+-----------------+         +-------------+

Adapter Pattern:

+----------+
|  Client  |
+-----+----+
      |
      v
+----------+
|  Target  |<-----------+
| interface|            |
+-----+----+            |
      | implements      |
      v                 |
+----------+            |
|  Adapter |------------+
+-----+----+
      | uses
      v
+----------+
|  Adaptee |
|specific  |
|Request() |
+----------+

Q23. Discuss how the Observer pattern is used in the Model-View-Controller (MVC) architecture.

Answer: MVC and Observer:

+-------------------------------------+
|              Model                  |
|         (ConcreteSubject)           |
|         - Business logic            |
|         - Application state         |
+--------------+----------------------+
               | notify
        +------+------+
        |             |
        v             v
+-----------+   +-----------+
|    View   |   | Controller|
| (Concrete |   |           |
|  Observer)|   |           |
| - Display |   | - Input   |
|   data    |   |   handling|
+-----------+   +-----------+

How it works: 1. Model contains data and business logic 2. Views register as observers of Model 3. When Model changes, it notifies all Views 4. Views update their display 5. Controllers handle user input and update Model

Benefits: - Multiple views of same data - Automatic synchronization - Loose coupling

Q24. Explain how the Adapter pattern can be used to integrate legacy code with new systems.

Answer: Scenario: New system needs functionality from legacy system, but interfaces are incompatible.

Solution: 1. Define interface expected by new system (Target) 2. Create Adapter that implements Target 3. Adapter wraps legacy system (Adaptee) 4. Adapter translates Target calls to Adaptee calls

Example:

// New system expects this interface
interface ModernPayment {
    void processPayment(PaymentDetails details);
}

// Legacy system has this interface
class LegacyPayment {
    void makePayment(double amount, String currency) { ... }
}

// Adapter bridges the gap
class PaymentAdapter implements ModernPayment {
    private LegacyPayment legacy;

    void processPayment(PaymentDetails details) {
        legacy.makePayment(
            details.getAmount(), 
            details.getCurrency()
        );
    }
}

Benefits: - No changes to legacy code - New system uses standard interface - Easy to replace legacy system later - Can add functionality in adapter

docs.title: BONUS: COMPREHENSIVE QUESTIONS - ANSWERS
docs.text:
Q1. You are asked to develop a new online banking system. Describe your approach.

Answer: Feasibility Study: - Technical: Assess security requirements, technology stack - Economic: Cost-benefit analysis, ROI calculation - Schedule: Determine realistic timeline

Process Model: - Choose Iterative/Agile approach - Banking requirements change frequently - Need early delivery of core features - Regulatory requirements need documentation

Requirements Gathering: - Interview bank staff and customers - Analyze existing systems - Create use cases: Transfer Funds, Pay Bills, View Statements - Define security and performance requirements

UML Diagrams: - Use case diagram: Show all banking functions - Class diagram: Account, Customer, Transaction classes - Sequence diagram: Fund transfer process - Activity diagram: Loan approval workflow - State diagram: Account states (Active, Frozen, Closed)

Design Patterns: - Facade: Simplify complex banking operations - Observer: Notify customers of transactions - Adapter: Integrate with legacy banking systems - Singleton: Database connection pool

Q2. Compare and contrast all the process models.

Answer: (See detailed comparison in Q16 of Process Models section)

Q3. Explain the complete process of requirements engineering.

Answer: Requirements Engineering Process:

  1. Elicitation:
  2. Identify stakeholders
  3. Select techniques (interviews, workshops, observation)

  4. Gather raw requirements

  5. Analysis:

  6. Classify requirements (functional, non-functional)
  7. Prioritize requirements
  8. Resolve conflicts

  9. Model requirements (use cases, domain models)

  10. Specification:

  11. Write SRS document
  12. Include use cases, diagrams

  13. Ensure quality criteria

  14. Validation:

  15. Review with stakeholders
  16. Check completeness, consistency

  17. Prototype for feedback

  18. Management:

  19. Track changes
  20. Maintain traceability
  21. Version control

Q4. Design a complete UML model for a system.

Answer: (Detailed UML diagrams would be drawn based on chosen system)

Q5. Discuss how design patterns contribute to software quality.

Answer: Software Quality Aspects:

  1. Maintainability:
  2. Patterns provide proven structure

  3. Easier to understand and modify

  4. Reusability:

  5. Pattern solutions are reusable

  6. Components can be reused

  7. Flexibility:

  8. Easy to extend (Observer, Adapter)

  9. Easy to modify (Facade)

  10. Reliability:

  11. Proven solutions reduce defects

  12. Well-tested approaches

  13. Scalability:

  14. Observer supports many observers
  15. Facade can handle growing subsystems

End of Answers - Good luck with your midsem exam!

docs.title: Key Points to Include in Answers
SE Introduction
docs.text:
• Software engineering is about solving customer problems, not just writing code
  • Four main activities: requirements, design, implementation, verification
  • Importance of customers vs. users

docs.title: Process Models
docs.text:
• Waterfall: Sequential, rigid, good for well-understood projects
  • Iterative: Allows feedback between phases
  • Prototyping: For exploring requirements
  • Incremental: Deliver in parts
  • Spiral: Risk-driven, iterative with explicit risk analysis
  • Agile: Lightweight, flexible, customer-focused

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Functional vs. non-functional requirements
  • Use cases capture functional requirements
  • SRS should be clear, unambiguous, verifiable, traceable

docs.title: UML Diagrams
docs.text:
• Use case: System functionality from user perspective
  • Class: Static structure with relationships
  • Sequence: Object interactions over time
  • State: Object lifecycle
  • Activity: Workflow/process flow

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Association: "knows a" relationship
  • Aggregation: "has a" (whole-part, parts can exist independently)
  • Composition: "contains a" (whole-part, parts cannot exist independently)
  • Generalization: "is a" relationship (inheritance)

docs.title: Design Patterns
docs.text:
• Facade: Simplified interface to a complex subsystem
  • Observer: One-to-many dependency, notification mechanism
  • Adapter: Convert one interface to another

Good luck with your midsem exam!

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
• Customer demands priority.
  • Requirements should be clear need not be complete
  • Changes can be accommodated
  • Good for objected oriented development
  • Large products

docs.title: Advantages
docs.text:
• Client gets important functionality (priority based)
  • Client has better idea about the project
  • Error debugging is easier
  • Changes can be accommodated easily
  • Flexible and less expensive
  • Risk handling is good
  • Flexible to changes

docs.title: Disadvantages
docs.text:
• Modular interface is necessary
  • Proper planning is necessary
  • Proper integration is mandatory

docs.title: Incremental Model OR Development Model
docs.text:
• divide the system into smaller parts
  • develop each part fully
  • deliver it
  • then add the next part
  • each increment is like a water fall
  • each increment goes through
    • requirements
    • design
    • implementation
    • testing
  • iterative in delivery
  • linear in each increment

docs.title: When to use
docs.text:
• Modular
  • All requirements are to be known firsthand
  • Fast demands of customer
  • Priority based development
  • funding is released in stages
  • high risk modules can be developed first
  • Initial delivery cost is less
  • Good for untrained developers
  • Long schedule
  • Web application and Product based companies

docs.title: When not to use
docs.text:
• system is very small
  • requirements are extremely unclear
  • architecture cannot be modularized

docs.title: Advantages
docs.text:
• Client gets important functionality (priority based)
  • Client has better idea about the project
  • Error debugging is easier
  • Changes can be accommodated easily
  • Flexible and less expensive
  • Risk handling is good

docs.title: Disadvantages
docs.text:
• Modular interface is necessary
  • Proper planning is necessary
  • Proper integration is mandatory

docs.title: WHICH STEP FIRST?
docs.text:
• Some steps will be pre-requisite because of physical dependencies
  • Others may be in any order
  • Value to cost ratios may be used
    • V/C where
    • V is a score 1-10 representing value to customer
    • C is a score 0-10 representing cost to developers

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
• Iterative changes to the software
  • First version of the software is developed after which reviews are considered, and changes are made to make another iteration.
  • If everything goes well, the product is deployed.

docs.title: When to use
docs.text:
• When the requirements are known.
  • When there are changes to requirements in future.
  • When the software is large.
  • A new technology is present and is learnt by the development team while developing
  • When there are high risk features present that have to be reviewed in future.

docs.title: Advantages
docs.text:
• Testing and debugging during smaller iteration is easy.
  • More time can be spend on designing and planning than documentation.
  • It easily accepts changes to the software after the initial iterations.
  • Risks are identified and can be changed in the next iteration.
  • There is a parallel planning team to review changes for the next iteration.

docs.title: Disadvantages
docs.text:
• It is not suitable for smaller projects.
  • More resources are required.
  • Project completion cannot be decided.
  • Requirement changes can have an affect to the budget.
  • More time consumed due to design changes in later iterations.

docs.title: 🔹 First: What is a Life Cycle?
docs.text:
A life cycle simply means:

The stages a software product goes through from birth to retirement.

Think of it like a human life:

Birth → Childhood → Youth → Adult → Old age

Similarly, software:

  • Feasibility

  • Requirements

  • Design

  • Coding

  • Testing

  • Maintenance

  • Retirement

That sequence is the software life cycle.

So a:

docs.title: 🔵 Life Cycle Model
docs.text:
Is a representation of the phases in the software’s life.

It answers:

  • What phases exist?

  • In what order?

  • When does a phase start and end?

  • What are the entry and exit criteria?

Example:

  • Waterfall

  • V-Model

  • Spiral

  • Agile

These are life cycle models because they describe how the product evolves through phases.

docs.title: 🔹 Now: What is a Process?
docs.text:
A process is more detailed.

A process means:

The complete set of activities, methods, practices, rules, and tools used to develop software.

It includes:

  • Phases

  • Activities inside phases

  • Roles

  • Responsibilities

  • Standards

  • Documentation formats

  • Tools

  • Review mechanisms

  • Metrics

So process is bigger than just phase sequence.

docs.title: 🔵 Process Model
docs.text:
A process model describes:

How development activities are carried out in practice.

It answers:

  • Who does what?

  • How is work assigned?

  • How are reviews done?

  • How is quality ensured?

  • What documents are produced?

  • How is progress tracked?

docs.title: 🔥 Core Difference (Simple Way)
docs.text: Life Cycle Model = Structure of phases Process Model = How work is actually performed within and across those phases

docs.title: 🔎 Analogy (Very Clear One)
docs.text:
Imagine building a house.

Life Cycle:

  • Planning

  • Designing

  • Construction

  • Inspection

  • Maintenance

Process:

  • Which architect?

  • What review method?

  • What documentation?

  • What construction standards?

  • What approval workflow?

  • Which tools used?

Life cycle is the skeleton. Process is the flesh and muscle.

docs.title: 🔬 More Technical Difference
docs.text: Aspect Life Cycle Model Process Model Focus Phases Activities + rules Scope High-level Detailed Answers What stages? How to execute work? Concern Product evolution Work management Includes roles? Not necessarily Yes Includes tools/standards? No Yes

docs.title: 🔥 Why Textbooks Mix Them
docs.text:
In many books (and even in your PDF), they say:

“Life cycle model (also called process model)”

Because early models like Waterfall described both:

  • Phase structure

  • Development flow

So they got treated as the same thing.

But strictly speaking:

  • Life cycle = conceptual stages

  • Process = implementation of development discipline

docs.title: 🧠 Example Using Waterfall
docs.text:
Waterfall as Life Cycle:

  • Sequential phases

Waterfall as Process:

  • Each phase has defined documentation

  • Entry/exit criteria

  • Review checkpoints

  • Deliverables

Same name — different abstraction levels.

docs.title: 🔥 Big Insight
docs.text:
Life cycle model answers:

How does the product evolve over time?

Process model answers:

How does the team work to build it?

docs.title: 🧩 In Modern Context
docs.text:
For example:

Agile:

Life cycle:

  • Iterative cycles (sprints)

Process:

  • Daily standups

  • Sprint planning

  • Backlog grooming

  • Retrospectives

  • CI/CD tools

docs.title: 🎯 Exam-Ready Definition
docs.text:
Life Cycle Model: A descriptive model that identifies and organizes the phases of software development.

Process Model: A comprehensive framework that defines the activities, roles, workflows, standards, and practices used during software development.

docs.title: ⚡ One-Line Memory Trick
docs.text: Life Cycle = Timeline Process = Work Discipline

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
• In this model, a prototype of the original software is created.
  • This is model is used when the user is not certain about the requirements.
  • It is "trial and error" method for SDLC.

docs.title: Advantages
docs.text:
• Prototype model does not have to know complete details about input, output and processes.
  • The prototype can change easily.
  • Perfect model when the customers are actively participating.
  • The prototype can be discarded easily if the the customer is not satisfied.
  • Flexible, can accommodate changes.
  • Errors can be detected easily.
  • Helps team member to communicate easily and understand specifications.

docs.title: Disadvantages
docs.text:
• Client involvement is more
  • It is a very slow process
  • Many changes can disturb the rhythm
  • Documentation is very poor due to constant changes
  • Costly in terms of time and money.
  • Prototyping tools are expensive.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
Aspect Waterfall Iterative Waterfall V-Model Prototyping Incremental Evolutionary Basic idea One phase after another Waterfall with feedback Dev + test in parallel Build prototype to refine reqs Build system in parts System evolves through versions Overall flow Strictly linear Semi-linear Linear with validation Cyclic Iterative Iterative & adaptive Requirement handling Fixed at start Mostly fixed Very clear & fixed Initially unclear Partially fixed Continuously evolving Handling changes Very difficult Moderate Difficult Very easy Easy Very easy Customer involvement Very low Low Low Very high Medium Very high Working software Only at end After iterations After coding Very early After each increment After each evolution Testing After development After each iteration Parallel with dev After prototype feedback Per increment Continuous Risk handling High risk Medium Medium Low Low Very low Documentation Heavy Heavy Very heavy Light Medium Light Flexibility Very low Medium Low Very high High Very high Best suited for Small, stable systems Medium stable systems Safety-critical systems Unclear requirements Large systems with clear modules Complex, changing systems Main advantage Simple & structured Controlled flexibility Strong verification Clearer requirements Early value delivery Adapts to change Main disadvantage No change support Still rigid Costly changes Prototype may mislead Needs good planning Hard to estimate

  • Waterfall → “One pass, no return”

  • Iterative Waterfall → “Waterfall with correction”

  • V-Model → “Build and test together”

  • Prototyping → “Build to understand”

  • Incremental → “Deliver in pieces” (Chain of waterfall)

  • Evolutionary → _“Grow and adapt continuously” (Incremental + Iterative)

docs.title: Use case
docs.text:
• More quality assurance is required
  • Used for critical systems
  • Waterfall-like model
  • Used for complex projects

docs.title: Advantages
docs.text:
• Disciplined model and phases are completed one by one.
  • Simple and easier to used.
  • Constant testing
  • Highly structured.
  • Clear communication between development and testing teams.

docs.title: Disadvantages
docs.text:
• Not good for complex and large products.
  • Not flexible to constant changes
  • No MVP created
  • Requirements has to be known initially
  • Poor documentation

docs.title: Water fall
docs.text:
Also known as linear sequential model - Requirements - Design - Development - Testing - Deployment - Maintenance

  • Every stage is completed before starting the next stage.
  • Only forward direction, no backward direction

Requirements Analysis, Design and Coding are considered as development phases

Among all phases, Maintenance takes the most effort and time Among the development phase, Testing takes the most effort and time

docs.title: When to use
docs.text:
• requirements are fixed (not changed)
  • Simple short projects
  • All tools and tech are consistent (not changed)
  • All resources are well prepared and are available

docs.title: Requirement Analysis
docs.text:
• Communication with customer and Stackholders

    • Functional requirements
      • What are the features the customer is expecting
    • Performance
    • UI UX
  • SRS is created
    • Contains detailed description on what user need
    • Contract between the development team and the customer

[!tip] This generates SRS = Software Requirements Specification

  • Class: OrderItem
  • Class: OrderService
  • Method: placeOrder()
  • Method: cancelOrder()
  • Relationship: Order → OrderItem

docs.title: Development Phase
docs.text:
• Design in translated to source code
  • Units are created and unit test is done. (each module is created and checked)

docs.title: Testing Phase
docs.text:
• Performs all the testing activities and check whether it meets the customers needs.

    [!tip] Generates Test Cases and Test Reports

docs.title: Deployment
docs.text: • Released in market

docs.title: Maintenance
docs.text:
• Fix the bugs
  • Adds new features

docs.title: Advantages
docs.text:
• Simple and easy to understand
  • Each phase completed to move to next phase
  • Works well in small projects
  • Requirements are very well understood and fixed
  • Process and results are documented properly

docs.title: Disadvantages
docs.text:
• High amount of risk and uncertainity
  • Can't go backward
  • Not flexible
  • Not good for complex projects
  • Client feedback loop cannot be included

docs.title: Aggregation
docs.text:
• "Is part of" relationship
  • Represents a whole part relationship
  • Represented by a diamond symbol
  • If parent is destroyed, child still lives

example: - Library has Books - Books can exist outside the library - Team has Players - Players can exist even if the team is disbanded

  • Symbol is hollow diamond in the parent side

docs.title: Association
docs.text:
• "knows a" relationship
  • allows communication between objects using its id (pointer)
  • Can be 1-1, 1-n, n-1, etc
  • Represented by a straight labelled line

docs.title: Association and Link
docs.text:
• An association is a class level relationship
  • Link is an object level relationship

docs.title: example:
docs.text:
• A Teacher teaches a student = Association
  • "Kiran" teaches "Alvin" = Link

docs.title: Qualified Association
docs.text:
• A qualified association is an association where you use a key (qualifier) to uniquely select one (or a subset of) related objects
  • Association + Lookup Key
  • Like ISBN of a book instead of the pointer to the book
  • We keep a map of qualifiers to pointers for lookup
  • Use of qualifier changes the cardinality

example: Library --- Book (0..*) Library --- [ISBN] --- Book (0..1)

Association comes when: - A delegates to B - A needs help from B - A and B are peers

docs.title: Composition
docs.text:
• "is made of" relationship
  • One class owns another completely
  • If parent is destroyed, child must die

example: - House has rooms - Room cannot exist without a house - Human's has heart - Heart belongs to that human completely

  • Symbol is filled diamond in the parent side

Composition comes where: - B is a permanent part of A - A contains B - A is a permanent collection of Bs

docs.title: Dependency
docs.text:
• One class uses another class temporarily
  • No field, no ownership
  • Short lived
  • Once task is done, relationship is gone
class Printer {
    void print() {}
}

class Report {
    void generate(Printer printer) {
        printer.print();
    }
}
  • Symbol is dotted arrow from dependent to independent class
  • Report - - - > Printer

docs.title: Stereotype in dependency
docs.text:
A dependency in UML means:

A change in the supplier may affect the client.

Stereotypes refine what kind of dependency it is.

The ones in your PDF are more formal UML ones (often used in model-level design, not just class diagrams).

docs.title: 🔹 Meaning
docs.text:
Relates two model elements that represent the same concept at different levels of abstraction.

In simple words:

One is a more detailed version of the other.

docs.title: 🔹 Example
docs.text:
Requirement: “System shall authenticate users.”

Design element: AuthenticationModule class.

The design is an abstraction refinement of the requirement.

Or:

High-level business model ↓ Detailed technical model

They represent the same concept, but at different abstraction levels.

docs.title: 🔹 Important Note
docs.text:
This is common in:

  • Model-driven development

  • Requirements → Design mapping

docs.title: 2️⃣ Binding — <<bind>>
docs.text: This one is slightly more technical.

docs.title: 🔹 Meaning
docs.text:
Used in template mechanisms.

It connects:

  • Template parameters to

  • Actual arguments

To create a specific model element.

docs.title: 🔹 Example (Generic Programming Concept)
docs.text:
Suppose you have a template class:

List<T>

Now you create:

List<Integer>

Here:

List<Integer> has a <<bind>> dependency on List<T>

Because we bind: T → Integer

docs.title: 🔹 Where Used?
docs.text:
Mostly in:

  • UML template modeling

  • Generic classes

  • Parameterized models

docs.title: 3️⃣ Realization — <<realize>>
docs.text: This is very important.

docs.title: 🔹 Meaning
docs.text:
The client implements the contract of the supplier.

This is basically:

Implementation of an interface.

docs.title: 🔹 Example
docs.text:
Interface: PaymentService

Class: CreditCardPayment

CreditCardPayment <<realize>> PaymentService

In UML, realization is often shown with a dashed line + hollow triangle arrow.

docs.title: 🔹 Important Clarification
docs.text: Realization is technically a specialized form of dependency, but UML gives it special notation because it’s very common.

docs.title: 4️⃣ Substitution — <<substitute>>
docs.text: This one is conceptually very nice.

docs.title: 🔹 Meaning
docs.text:
The client can replace the supplier.

It indicates substitutability.

docs.title: 🔹 Example
docs.text:
Suppose:

Base component: Logger

Alternative component: FileLogger

If FileLogger can replace Logger without breaking the system:

FileLogger <<substitute>> Logger

docs.title: 🔹 Real-World Meaning
docs.text:
This reflects:

Liskov Substitution Principle (from OOP)

If B is a subtype of A, Objects of A can be replaced by objects of B.

docs.title: 🔥 Now Let’s Compare All Four Clearly
docs.text: Stereotype What It Means Where Used <<abstraction>> Same concept, different abstraction levels Requirement → Design <<bind>> Template parameter binding Generic/template classes <<realize>> Implements interface/contract Class implements interface <<substitute>> Can replace another element Polymorphism / Subtyping

docs.title: 🔹 Conceptual Hierarchy Insight
docs.text:
All four are:

Specialized forms of dependency.

But they represent different semantic meanings:

  • Abstraction → conceptual refinement

  • Bind → parameter instantiation

  • Realize → implementation

  • Substitute → replaceability

docs.title: 🔥 Important Clarification
docs.text:
These stereotypes are mostly used in:

  • Class diagrams

  • Component diagrams

  • Model-driven architecture (MDA)

  • Advanced UML modeling

In basic academic UML, professors usually expect:

  • <<use>>

  • <<create>>

  • <<realize>>

But your PDF is covering more formal UML 2.x semantics.

docs.title: 🔹 Clean Final Summary
docs.text:
Dependency stereotypes refine the nature of dependency.

From your PDF:

  • <<abstraction>> → Different levels of same concept

  • <<bind>> → Template parameter binding

  • <<realize>> → Implementation of contract

  • <<substitute>> → One element can replace another

All are special kinds of dependency relationships.

docs.title: Inheritance
docs.text:
• "has a " relationship
  • Car is a Vehicle
  • Human is an Animal
  • Represented by an arrow towards the parent

docs.title: Discriminators
docs.text:
• Can be used to separate child classes into clusters
  • Here issuable and reference are discriminators

docs.title: Disadvantages
docs.text:
• Tight coupling
  • Overuse can result in poor quality of code

Inheritance comes where: - A is a kind of B - A is a specialization of B - A behaves like B

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Relationship Keyword Lifetime Ownership Example Inheritance IS-A Same N/A Car is Vehicle Association KNOWS-A Independent None Teacher–Student Aggregation PART-OF Independent Weak Library–Book Composition MADE-OF Dependent Strong Car–Engine Dependency USES-A Temporary None Report–Printer

docs.title: Interface
docs.text: • Interfaces are also represented as Filled Circles

docs.title: Types of Requirement Modeling
docs.text:
• Scenario-Based Models

    • Describe system from user perspective.
    • Example: Use Cases

  • Data Models

    • Focus on data structure and relationships.

  • Class-Oriented Models

    • Focus on classes, objects, attributes, relationships.
    • Example: Class Diagram

  • Flow-Oriented Models

    • Focus on data flow through system.
    • Example: Data Models, Data Flow Diagram

  • Behavioral Models

    • Focus on system behavior over time (state changes, activities).
    • Example: State Diagram, Sequence Diagram

docs.title: Structural Diagrams
docs.text: • These describes what the system is

docs.title: Class Diagram
docs.text:
• Shows:
    • Classes
    • Attribute
    • Method
    • Relationship

docs.title: Object Diagram
docs.text:
• Shows:
    • Instances of classes
    • Relationships between objects

docs.title: Component Diagram
docs.text:
• Shows:
    • Logical grouping of components

docs.title: Deployment Diagram
docs.text:
• Shows:
    • Physical hardware nodes
    • Where components are deployed

docs.title: Behavioral Diagram
docs.text: • These describes how the system behaves

docs.title: Use Case Diagram
docs.text: • High level user goals and interactions

docs.title: Sequence Diagram
docs.text: • Shows time order of messages between objects

docs.title: Collaboration Diagram
docs.text: • Shows structure of object interactions

docs.title: State Chart Diagram
docs.text: • Shows state changes triggered by events

docs.title: Activity Diagram
docs.text:
• Shows flow of control between activities
Purpose Diagrams Requirements Use Case Structure Class Diagram Behavior Activity, State Machine, Interaction

docs.title: 1️⃣ STRUCTURAL DIAGRAMS
docs.text:
Structural diagrams model the static structure of the system — the elements that exist and how they relate to each other.

These diagrams answer:

  • What are the main components?

  • What are the data structures?

  • How are elements connected?

The main structural diagrams used in requirement modelling are:

• Class Diagram • Object Diagram • Component Diagram • Deployment Diagram

docs.title: 1.1 Class Diagram
docs.text:
A Class Diagram shows:

  • Classes

  • Attributes (data members)

  • Methods (functions)

  • Relationships between classes

It represents the logical structure of the system.

It focuses on:

  • What objects exist?

  • What data do they store?

  • How are they related?

Example: Library Management System

Classes:

  • Book

  • Borrower

  • Librarian

  • Loan

Relationships:

  • A Borrower borrows a Book

  • A Librarian manages Books

  • A Loan connects Borrower and Book

Example structure:

Class: Book Attributes:

  • bookID

  • title

  • author

  • status

Class: Borrower Attributes:

  • borrowerID

  • name

  • membershipType

Relationship: Borrower —— borrows —— Book

This diagram helps identify:

  • Entities in the system

  • Data organization

  • Object relationships (association, aggregation, composition, inheritance)

Why it is important in requirements: Because it clarifies what data and domain concepts exist before implementation.

docs.title: 1.2 Object Diagram
docs.text:
An Object Diagram shows instances of classes at a particular moment in time.

If a class diagram shows the blueprint, an object diagram shows the real objects.

Example:

book1 : Book title = "Software Engineering" status = "Available"

borrower1 : Borrower name = "Alvin"

loan1 : Loan

It shows:

  • Actual object values

  • Snapshot of system state

  • Real-time configuration

Used when:

  • You want to understand a scenario concretely.

  • You want to test whether your class diagram makes sense.

docs.title: 1.3 Component Diagram
docs.text:
A Component Diagram shows high-level modules and their dependencies.

It focuses on:

  • Logical grouping of functionality

  • Subsystems

  • Interfaces between modules

Example: Course Registration System

Components:

  • Registration Module

  • Billing Module

  • Authentication Module

  • Database

Relationships: Registration Module → Billing Module Registration Module → Database

This diagram helps in:

  • Understanding system architecture

  • Dividing responsibilities

  • Planning development teams

docs.title: 1.4 Deployment Diagram
docs.text:
A Deployment Diagram shows the physical layout of the system.

It answers:

  • Where is the software deployed?

  • What hardware nodes exist?

  • How are they connected?

Example:

Client Machine → Web Server → Application Server → Database Server

In an ATM System:

ATM Machine → Bank Server → Central Database

It models:

  • Nodes (hardware)

  • Communication links

  • Software artifacts deployed on nodes

Important during:

  • System architecture planning

  • Distributed systems modelling

docs.title: 2️⃣ BEHAVIORAL DIAGRAMS
docs.text:
Behavioral diagrams describe how the system behaves over time.

They answer:

  • What actions occur?

  • In what sequence?

  • How does the system react to events?

  • What are the workflows?

Major behavioral diagrams:

• Use Case Diagram • Sequence Diagram • Collaboration Diagram • State Chart Diagram • Activity Diagram

docs.title: 2.1 Use Case Diagram
docs.text:
This is the most important diagram in requirement modelling.

A Use Case Diagram shows:

  • Actors (users or external systems)

  • Use cases (functionalities)

  • Relationships between them

It focuses on: "What does the system do for the user?"

Example: ATM System

Actor:

  • Customer

Use Cases:

  • Insert Card

  • Withdraw Cash

  • Check Balance

  • Deposit Money

Relationships: Customer → Withdraw Cash Customer → Check Balance

Extensions: "Print Receipt" extends "Withdraw Cash"

Include: "Authenticate User" included in "Withdraw Cash"

Use case diagrams:

  • Capture functional requirements

  • Identify system scope

  • Help in requirement validation

docs.title: 2.2 Sequence Diagram
docs.text:
A Sequence Diagram shows interaction between objects over time.

It focuses on:

  • Order of messages

  • Timeline of events

Example: ATM Withdraw

  1. Customer → ATM : insertCard()

  2. ATM → BankServer : validateCard()

  3. BankServer → ATM : approval

  4. ATM → Customer : requestAmount()

  5. ATM → BankServer : deductAmount()

The vertical axis represents time.

Used to:

  • Understand detailed interaction flow

  • Validate logic of a use case

docs.title: 2.3 Collaboration Diagram (Communication Diagram)
docs.text:
A Collaboration Diagram also shows interactions between objects.

Difference from sequence diagram:

  • Focuses on structural organization

  • Emphasizes object relationships

  • Messages are numbered to show order

Example:

Customer — ATM — BankServer

Messages:

  1. insertCard

  2. validateCard

  3. approve

Used to:

  • Understand object responsibility

  • Analyze object relationships during interaction

docs.title: 2.4 State Chart Diagram
docs.text:
A State Chart Diagram shows state changes of an object in response to events.

It is event-driven.

It answers:

  • What states can an object be in?

  • What causes state transitions?

Example: Order System

States:

  • Created

  • Paid

  • Shipped

  • Delivered

  • Cancelled

Transitions: Created → Paid (after payment received) Paid → Shipped (after dispatch) Shipped → Delivered

This is very important when:

  • System behavior depends on states

  • Complex workflows exist

  • Real-time systems are involved

docs.title: 2.5 Activity Diagram
docs.text:
An Activity Diagram shows workflow or flow of control.

It is similar to a flowchart but more powerful.

It shows:

  • Activities

  • Decisions

  • Parallel processes

  • Start and end points

Example: Course Registration

Start → Login → View Courses → Select Course → Check Availability → Available? Yes → Register No → Display Error → End

It supports:

  • Parallel flows (fork/join)

  • Decision nodes

  • Swimlanes (who performs what)

Used for:

  • Business process modelling

  • Complex workflows

  • Algorithm visualization

docs.title: Structural vs Behavioral – Clear Comparison
docs.text: Aspect Structural Diagrams Behavioral Diagrams Focus What exists What happens Nature Static Dynamic Shows Classes, objects, components Interactions, workflows, states Time factor No Yes Used for Data & architecture modelling Functional and dynamic modelling

docs.title: Why Both Are Needed
docs.text:
If you only model structure: You know what classes exist, but not how they behave.

If you only model behavior: You know workflows, but not how data is organized.

Good requirement modelling requires both.

Because as the principle says:

“If a requirement cannot be modeled, it is not fully understood.”

docs.title: Use Case Diagram
docs.text:
• A use case is typically sequence of actions that an actor performs in order to complete a given task
  • Who interacts with the system = Actor
  • What does the system provides = Use Case
